- Motors, gearboxes, sensors: ~35 kg (29%) - partial (need magnets, precision)

Assembly time: ~140 hours (8 phases from base to testing/calibration)

breakdown of robot subsystems based on industrial manipulator architecture.

raw.name: Hydrogen-oxygen torch
raw.notes:
Hydrogen-oxygen flame torch for high-temperature applications.
Produces flame temperature ~2800°C through H2-O2 combustion.
Primary applications:
  - Flame hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride (SiCl4 → SiO2 + HCl)
  - High-purity fused silica glass production
  - Chemical vapor deposition processes
Components:
  - Gas mixing chamber with flow controls
  - Flame nozzle/burner head (refractory materials)
  - Safety interlocks and flashback arrestors
  - Pressure regulators for H2 and O2 feeds
Operating principle:
  - 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O + heat (exothermic combustion)
  - Flame temperature regulated by H2:O2 ratio
  - Typical ratio 2:1 (stoichiometric)
Safety features:
  - Flashback arrestors prevent flame propagation into gas lines
  - Pressure monitoring and automatic shutoff
  - Explosion-proof construction
Used in silica_glass_high_purity_v0 process.
Assumptions: Mass aligned with recipe input mass (~18.42 kg).

raw.name: General labor bot (automation)
raw.notes:
6-DOF industrial robotic manipulator for lunar manufacturing operations.

Design specification: docs/labor_bot_design_memo.md

Key specifications:

- Reach: 2.0 m workspace radius
- Payload: 20 kg at full extension
- Repeatability: ±0.5 mm
- Degrees of freedom: 6 (full 3D position + orientation)

Architecture:
- Mechanical structure: Aluminum/steel links and housings (35 kg)

- Power system: 48V DC from 240V 3-phase AC supply (8 kg)

- Sensing: Stereo cameras, 6-axis force sensor, encoders (12 kg)
- Integration: Cables, thermal management, safety systems (21 kg)

Lunar manufacturability:
- Structures, cables, thermal: ~46% (lunar Al/Fe/Cu)
- Motors, gearboxes: ~29% (need magnets, precision)
- Electronics, sensors: ~25% (Earth import)

Assembly time: ~140 hours with all parts available
Power consumption: 825W average, 2.7kW peak
Service life: 10,000 hours before major overhaul

Operates inside pressurized habitat (not EVA-rated). Provides versatile
manipulation for assembly, material handling, quality inspection, and
machine operation tasks.

raw.notes:
Krypton gas (Kr) extracted from lunar regolith volatiles.

Properties:
- Atomic number: 36
- Atomic mass: 83.80 amu
- Boiling point: 119.9 K (-153°C)
- Noble gas (chemically inert)
- Colorless, odorless, non-flammable

Sources on Moon:
- Solar wind implantation in regolith
- Concentration: ~0.02 ppm (extremely low)
- Requires processing vast quantities of regolith

Applications:
- Ion engine propellant (alternative to xenon)
- Inert atmosphere and specialized lighting
- Leak detection tracer gas

Production:
- Multi-stage cryogenic distillation
- Separation from Ar and Xe by boiling point
- Energy intensive: ~200 kWh/kg

Lunar context:

Density: ~1.99 g/cm³ (Mg2Si intermetallic)

  - Semiconductor: Narrow-gap semiconductor
  - Hydrogen storage: Can absorb/release H2

  - Intermetallic compound (not mechanical mixture)
  - Improves strength, hardness, creep resistance in Al
  - Stable in vacuum (unlike pure Mg)
Composition varies with olivine Mg/Fe ratio:
  - Pure forsterite (Mg2SiO4): ~63% Mg, ~37% Si
  - Mixed olivine: May contain Fe (MgFeSi alloy)
Advantages: Direct one-step production from olivine
  Multiple applications (alloying, thermoelectric, H2 storage)
  More stable than pure Mg in lunar vacuum
Disadvantages: Variable composition depending on source
  Not suitable for applications requiring pure Mg or Si
Lunar context: Olivine in crater ejecta and maria
  Mg2Si valuable for Al alloy strengthening
  Thermoelectric potential for power generation

raw.name: Polar PSC Regolith (Ice-Bearing)
raw.description:
Ice-bearing regolith from permanently shadowed craters (PSCs) at lunar poles.

Contains significant water ice deposits (5.6% ± 2.9% by mass) mixed with
silicate regolith. Ice is rock-hard at PSC temperatures (~40 K / -233°C).

When ice-cemented, this material is extremely hard (similar to concrete)
and requires specialized drilling equipment for excavation.

physical_properties.notes:
Ice-cemented regolith in PSCs. Extremely hard when frozen.
Composition (excluding ice) similar to mixed highlands/mare regolith.
Density higher than dry regolith due to ice cement filling pores.

raw.notes:
Permanently shadowed crater (PSC) regolith from lunar poles.

Source: LCROSS impact data (Cabeus crater, south pole)
Water ice concentration: 5.6% by mass (range: 2.7% - 8.5%)
Temperature: ~40 K (-233°C) in permanent shadow

Location characteristics:
- North and south pole PSCs
- Total PSC area: >31,000 km² (both poles)
- Estimated ice inventory: 3-6 × 10¹² kg (3-6 billion tonnes)
- Cabeus crater: High concentration region
- 40+ craters at north pole with ice potential

Physical properties:
- Ice-cemented when frozen (rock-hard, similar to drilling concrete)
- Subsurface ice insulated by dry regolith overburden
- May be in layers or pockets (not uniformly distributed)
- Ice characteristics depend on depth and local geology

Operational challenges:
- Extreme cold (40 K requires special equipment)
- Permanently dark (no direct sunlight, requires heliostats or nuclear power)
- Rugged terrain (South Pole-Aitken basin: 11 km elevation changes)
- Hard drilling (ice-cemented material)

Compositional notes:
- Base regolith composition (excluding ice) assumed mixed highlands/mare
- PSCs can occur in both highland and mare regions
- Actual composition varies by specific PSC location
- 5.6% is average concentration; range 2.7% - 8.5% observed

raw.name: Steel drill string
raw.notes:
Steel drill pipe sections for drilling operations.

Drill string consists of:
- Drill pipe sections: Heavy-wall seamless steel tubes
- Tool joints: Threaded connections between sections
- Typical section: 3-6m length, 50-100mm diameter
- Wall thickness: 8-15mm for strength and torque transmission

Function:
- Transmit rotary motion from surface to drill bit
- Provide hydraulic conduit for drill fluid circulation
- Enable addition/removal of sections as hole deepens
- Withstand tension, compression, and torsion loads

Construction:
- Material: High-strength steel (often alloy steel)
- Threaded ends (API standard or proprietary threads)
- Internal upset for strength at connections
- Surface hardening for wear resistance

Lunar drilling context:
- Drilling into frozen regolith at polar craters
- Rock-hard ice at ~40K requires robust drill string
- Typical depth: 0.5-2 meters for water ice extraction
- Mass estimate: 100 kg for complete drill string set

Source: ai_estimate based on drilling industry standards
Scaled for lunar regolith/ice drilling application

raw.notes:

Technology: Multi-turn absolute encoder with magnetic or optical sensing.

raw.notes:

Technology: Incremental encoder with optical or magnetic quadrature sensing.

raw.name: Optical flat mirror

Flat optical mirror for microscope illumination path.

Imported due to precision optics manufacturing requirements:
- Optical-grade glass substrate (low defects, homogeneous)
- Precision grinding and polishing (λ/10 surface flatness, <10nm RMS roughness)
- Optical coating deposition (aluminum or silver, vacuum deposition)
- Interferometric metrology for surface quality verification
- Clean room environment to prevent contamination

Manufacturing requirements:
- Surface flatness: Better than λ/10 (wavelength/10, ~60nm for visible light)
- Surface roughness: <10nm RMS (for good reflectivity)
- Coating: Vacuum-deposited aluminum (88-92% reflectivity) or silver (>95%)
- Coating thickness: 100-200nm aluminum or 80-120nm silver
- Protective overcoat: SiO2 or other dielectric (optional, prevents oxidation)

Applications:
- Microscope illumination (beam steering, fold mirrors)
- Optical metrology systems
- Laser beam steering
- Interferometry reference surfaces

Local manufacturing path (future, advanced):
- Basalt glass substrate production (lower quality than commercial optical glass)
- CNC grinding and polishing (requires precision machine tools)
- Vacuum deposition system for reflective coating
- Interferometric testing equipment
- Still challenging for early lunar base due to precision requirements

For early bootstrapping, high-quality optical flats must be imported.

raw.notes:

Prevents accidental contact with rotating motors, gears, and pinch points
between moving arm segments. Required by machinery safety directives.

Components:
- Motor covers (6×): Enclosures for each joint motor/gearbox
  - Material: Polycarbonate (transparent) or aluminum sheet
  - Fastening: Tool-required (screws) to prevent casual removal
  - Ventilation: Slots or perforations (if motors need air cooling)
- Cable guards: Protective shields over cable routing paths
- Gripper finger guards: Prevent pinching between gripper jaws
- Joint covers: Prevent access to rotating joints

Design considerations:
- Must not interfere with robot motion (adequate clearance)
- Tool-required removal (prevents bypassing during operation)
- Visual access for inspection (transparent where possible)
- Easy removal for maintenance

Materials:
- Polycarbonate sheet: 3mm thick, impact-resistant (preferred for visibility)
- Aluminum sheet: 2mm thick (opaque but durable)
- Stainless steel mesh: For ventilated covers

Manufacturing: Sheet metal forming or polymer thermoforming. Polycarbonate
likely import initially. Aluminum from lunar resources. Fasteners (screws)
from steel.

raw.name: Safety light curtain
raw.notes:
Optical safety light curtain for industrial robot work cell protection.

Creates invisible barrier of infrared light beams. If person enters protected
area (breaking beams), robot immediately stops.

Specifications:
- Type: Type 4 safety light curtain (IEC 61496)
- Coverage: 2m × 2m work cell perimeter
- Resolution: 30 mm (minimum detectable object)
- Response time: <100 ms (detection to safety output)
- Range: Up to 5m between emitter and receiver
- Safety rating: SIL 2, Category 3 (ISO 13849)

Components:
- Emitter unit:
  - Array of infrared LEDs (850 nm wavelength)
  - Synchronization electronics
  - Mounting bracket
- Receiver unit:
  - Array of photodiodes aligned with emitter LEDs
  - Signal processing (detects beam interruption)
  - Safety output relay (dual-channel)
  - Status indicators (green = OK, red = beam blocked)
- Mounting posts (2×): Vertical posts at work cell corners
- Controller/interface module:
  - Connects to safety PLC
  - Provides muting and blanking functions
  - Configuration switches

Operation: If any beam blocked, safety output opens within 100ms, triggering
Safe Torque Off to robot. Green light indicates system operational.

Manufacturing: Optoelectronics (LEDs, photodiodes) import required.
Signal processing electronics import. Mounting hardware from lunar aluminum.

Design reference: docs/labor_bot_design_memo.md section 3.8.2.

raw.notes:

must be conducted from motors to radiator for radiative dissipation.

  - Length: ~1m each from joint to base
  - Diameter: 10mm
  - Working fluid: water or ammonia (sealed, evacuated)
  - Mass: ~1 kg total
- Aluminum radiator fins: Mounted on robot base
  - Surface area: 0.3 m²
  - Fin spacing: 10 mm
  - Mass: 0.8 kg
- Thermal interface pads: Between motor housing and heat pipe
  - Graphite or silicone-based
  - Mass: 0.2 kg

Heat dissipation capacity: 500W continuous (motors at 50% duty cycle).

Operation: Heat conducted from motor → heat pipe evaporates fluid → vapor
flows to radiator → condenses, releasing heat → radiates to environment →
liquid returns to motor end.

Manufacturing: Copper and aluminum from lunar resources. Heat pipe
fabrication requires vacuum sealing and fluid charging (specialized).

raw.notes:
Aluminosilicate glass production from lunar mineral oxides.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt
Composition: 57% SiO2, 20% Al2O3, 12% MgO, 5% CaO, 6% FeO
Melting point: 1100-1350°C (significantly lower than pure fused silica at 1710°C)
Purpose: Structural glass for habitats, greenhouses, and general applications
Lower melting point than pure silica saves energy
Process details:
  1. Gather oxide components from mineral processing:
     - SiO2: From anorthite leaching or direct silica extraction
     - Al2O3: From anorthite leaching + HCl calcination
     - MgO: From olivine processing or FFC by-product
     - CaO: From anorthite processing or lime extraction
     - FeO: From ilmenite reduction or iron oxidation (optional for color)
  2. Mix oxides in correct proportions
  3. Load into glass melting furnace (crucible_refractory or tank furnace)
  4. Heat to 1100-1350°C (above liquidus temperature)
  5. Maintain molten state for homogenization (1-3 hours)
  6. Stir or bubble to ensure uniform composition
  7. Form glass: Pour, cast, blow, or draw into desired shape
  8. Anneal: Slow cooling to relieve thermal stress (400-600°C)
  9. Final cooling to room temperature
Products:
  - Aluminosilicate glass: Transparent to translucent, greenish tint from FeO
  - Volatiles: Minor losses from evaporation
Composition details:
  - SiO2 (57%): Network former, provides structure
  - Al2O3 (20%): Improves durability, chemical resistance
  - MgO (12%): Flux, reduces melting point
  - CaO (5%): Flux, improves workability
  - FeO (6%): Natural lunar component, causes green/brown color
Glass properties:
  - Melting point: 1100-1350°C (depends on exact composition)
  - Density: ~2.5-2.7 g/cm³
  - Thermal expansion: Moderate (lower than soda-lime glass)
  - Chemical resistance: Excellent (aluminosilicate glasses durable)
  - Optical: Transparent but with greenish tint from FeO
Iron content and color:
  - Natural lunar glass contains FeO (reduces from Fe2O3 in vacuum melting)
  - FeO gives green to brown coloration
  - For transparent colorless glass: Must remove iron impurities
  - For colored glass: Can adjust FeO content deliberately
Decolorization (if needed):
  - Oxidize FeO to Fe2O3 (amber color, less intense)
  - Add MnO2 (complementary color, visual cancellation)
  - Or purify feedstock to remove all iron
Applications:
  - Habitat windows: Structural glazing, pressure barriers
  - Greenhouse covers: Transmit light for plant growth
  - Containers: Chemical-resistant glassware
  - Fiber optics: Draw into fibers (if purified)
  - Insulation: Spin into glass wool
  - Radiation shielding: High-density glass with heavy elements
Advantages: Lower melting point than pure silica (saves energy)
  Uses natural lunar mineral ratios (close to anorthite composition)
  No exotic additives required
  Durable and chemically resistant
  Can be formed by standard glass-working techniques
Disadvantages: Natural FeO content darkens glass
  Not suitable for precision optics (unless purified)
  Requires multiple oxide inputs (logistical complexity)
  Thermal shock sensitivity (needs careful annealing)
Comparison to fused silica:
  - Fused silica: 100% SiO2, melts at 1710°C, ultra-pure, expensive
  - Aluminosilicate: Mixed oxides, melts at 1100-1350°C, natural, economical
  - Fused silica for optics, aluminosilicate for structural
Comparison to soda-lime glass (Earth):
  - Soda-lime: 70% SiO2, 15% Na2O, 10% CaO, melts at 1000°C
  - Aluminosilicate: No Na2O (sodium scarce on Moon)
  - Higher Al2O3 content improves durability
Lunar context: Natural composition close to anorthite mineral
  Anorthite: CaAl2Si2O8 (decomposed to oxides)
  Add MgO from olivine, FeO from ilmenite
  Enables large-scale glass production from local resources
Glass forming techniques:
  - Casting: Pour into molds (flat sheets, blocks)
  - Blowing: Traditional glassblowing for complex shapes
  - Drawing: Pull fibers or rods from molten glass
  - Float process: Flat glass on molten tin bath (high quality)
  - Pressing: Mold under pressure (optical elements)
Annealing importance:
  - Glass cools unevenly → internal stress
  - Stress causes spontaneous fracture
  - Anneal at ~500°C (below glass transition)
  - Slow cool over hours to relieve stress
Thermal properties:
  - Coefficient of thermal expansion: ~5-7 × 10⁻⁶ /°C
  - Glass transition temperature: ~600-700°C
  - Softening point: ~800-900°C
  - Working range: 1000-1200°C
Chemical durability:
  - Excellent resistance to water, acids (except HF)
  - Aluminosilicate glasses very durable
  - Suitable for long-term lunar environment
Optical properties:
  - Refractive index: ~1.52-1.55
  - Transmittance: 80-90% (visible), reduced by FeO
  - Absorption edge: UV region (glass blocks UV)
Radiation resistance:
  - Glass darkens under ionizing radiation (color centers)
  - Aluminosilicate glasses more resistant than soda-lime
  - Can self-anneal under solar heating
Recycling:
  - Glass fully recyclable (remelt and reform)
  - No chemical degradation from multiple cycles
  - Broken glass (cullet) used as feedstock
Compositional flexibility:
  - Can adjust ratios for specific properties
  - More SiO2: Higher melting point, harder, more brittle
  - More MgO/CaO: Lower melting point, easier working
  - More Al2O3: Higher durability, chemical resistance
Advanced variants:
  - Borosilicate: Add B2O3 for thermal shock resistance (Pyrex-like)
  - Lead glass: Add PbO for high refractive index (optics)
  - But exotic additives may not be available initially
Scale-up potential:
  - Glass production highly scalable
  - Continuous tank furnaces for large-scale production
  - Can produce tons per day with proper infrastructure

raw.name: Ammonia recovery from ammonium chloride via CaO

energy_model.notes: Moderate heating for thermal decomposition, exothermic CaO reaction (3.0 kWh/kg * 1.0 kg NH4Cl)

time_model.notes: Thermal decomposition and ammonia recovery

raw.notes:
Ammonia recovery from ammonium chloride using calcium oxide (Solvay process recycling).
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: 2NH4Cl + CaO → 2NH3 + CaCl2 + H2O
Temperature: Moderate heating (200-400°C)
Purpose: Regenerate ammonia from Solvay process by-product for reuse in Haber-Bosch
Produces CaCl2 which replenishes FFC Cambridge electrolyte
Process details:
  1. Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) from Solvay process by-product
  2. Calcium oxide (CaO, quicklime) from anorthite or limestone
  3. Mix NH4Cl and CaO in rotary kiln or reactor
  4. Heat to 200-400°C
  5. NH4Cl + CaO → NH3 (gas) + CaCl2 + H2O
  6. Ammonia gas driven off by heat
  7. Capture NH3 gas via condensation or absorption
  8. Calcium chloride and water remain as solid/liquid
  9. Dry CaCl2 for use as FFC electrolyte
Products:
  - Ammonia gas (NH3): 63.6% by mass (recycled to Haber-Bosch)
  - Calcium chloride (CaCl2): Anhydrous form, 207.5% by mass of NH4Cl input
  - Water vapor: 33.8% by mass
Stoichiometry: 2NH4Cl (107g) + CaO (56.1g) → 2NH3 (34g) + CaCl2 (111g) + H2O (18g)
Per kg NH4Cl: 0.636 kg NH3, 2.075 kg CaCl2 (includes CaO input mass), 0.338 kg H2O
Note: CaCl2 mass includes both Cl from NH4Cl and Ca from CaO
Reaction characteristics:
  - Exothermic when CaO hydrates
  - NH3 release endothermic (requires heating)
  - Net: Slightly exothermic overall
Solvay process integration:
  - Solvay: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl
  - This process: NH4Cl + CaO → NH3 (recycled) + CaCl2
  - Overall: 97-98% NH3 recovery efficiency
  - NH3 is recycling reagent, not consumed
CaCl2 uses:
  - FFC Cambridge electrolyte: Primary use
  - Desiccant: Moisture absorption
  - De-icing: Road treatment (Earth applications)
  - Can be recycled to CaO + HCl if needed
Advantages: Recovers valuable NH3 for recycling
  Converts waste NH4Cl to useful CaCl2
  Replenishes FFC electrolyte stock
  Simple thermal process, no exotic reagents
  High recovery efficiency (>95%)
Disadvantages: Requires CaO input (consumable)
  Produces water that may need separation
  Moderate energy for heating
Lunar context: Critical for nitrogen conservation
  Nitrogen extremely scarce on Moon (ppb in volatiles)
  Must recycle NH3 with high efficiency
  Ammonia used in multiple processes:
    - Haber-Bosch (regenerates N2 → NH3)
    - Solvay process (Na2CO3 production)
    - Ostwald process (HNO3 production)
  CaCl2 by-product valuable for FFC electrolyte
Alternative ammonia recovery:
  - NH4Cl → NH3 + HCl (direct thermal decomposition)
  - Requires higher temperature (338°C sublimation)
  - Produces HCl which can be useful separately
  - CaO route preferred when CaCl2 is desired
Process optimization:
  - Use excess CaO to ensure complete NH3 liberation
  - Capture NH3 in water (aqueous ammonia solution)
  - Or cryogenic condensation (liquid NH3 at -33°C)
  - Dry CaCl2 thoroughly (hygroscopic, absorbs moisture)
Calcium oxide sources (lunar):
  - Anorthite leaching/processing: CaO by-product
  - Carbothermal reduction: CaAl2Si2O8 + C → CaO + Al2O3 + Si
  - Thermal decomposition: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (if carbonates available)
Nitrogen mass balance (Solvay + recovery):
  - N atoms in: NH3 (Solvay input)
  - N atoms out: NH3 (recovered from NH4Cl)
  - Net consumption: ~2-3% loss per cycle
  - Must make up with Haber-Bosch from volatiles
Integration with chlorine chemistry:
  - NaCl → HCl → various chlorides → recycling
  - NH3 enables NaCl utilization via Solvay
  - CaCl2 enables FFC metal extraction
  - Closed-loop system minimizes reagent imports
Temperature control:
  - Too low (<200°C): Incomplete NH3 liberation
  - Optimal (250-350°C): Good NH3 recovery, manageable
  - Too high (>400°C): May decompose CaCl2 to CaO + Cl2
Safety considerations:
  - NH3 is toxic and corrosive
  - Must contain and capture all NH3 gas
  - Proper ventilation and scrubbing systems
  - CaO is caustic (handle with care)
Yield optimization:
  - Molar ratio: 2 NH4Cl : 1 CaO (stoichiometric)
  - Slight excess CaO (5-10%) ensures complete reaction
  - Ammonia recovery: >95% typical

Disadvantages: Very high temperature, requires carbon feedstock
Product separation complexity

Lime-soda process for extracting alumina from anorthite feldspar.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Primary reaction: CaAl2Si2O8 + 3CaCO3 + Na2CO3 → 2NaAlO2 + 2Ca2SiO4 + 4CO2
Secondary processing:
  1. NaAlO2 + 2H2O → NaOH + Al(OH)3 (hydrolysis)
  2. 2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2O (calcination at 1050°C)
Temperature: Elevated for sintering/calcination
Process: Complex multi-stage chemical processing
Products:
  - Sodium aluminate (NaAlO2) - further processed to alumina
  - Calcium silicate (Ca2SiO4) - cement component, waste product
  - Carbon dioxide - evolved gas, can be captured
Advantages: Proven terrestrial process for alumina from non-bauxite sources
Anorthite used commercially on Earth via this route
Disadvantages: Very complex multi-step process
Requires Na2CO3 import/recycling (scarce on Moon)
Multiple processing stages with intermediate separations
Lower yield and efficiency than carbothermal route
Conclusion: TOO COMPLEX for first-generation lunar ISRU
Included for completeness and future consideration
Carbothermal reduction or HCl leaching preferred for lunar application
Stoichiometry: CaAl2Si2O8 (278.2g) + 3CaCO3 (300g) + Na2CO3 (106g) → 2NaAlO2 (164g) + 2Ca2SiO4 (348g) + 4CO2 (176g)
Final alumina yield: ~36.7% of anorthite mass (after hydrolysis and calcination)
May be viable for Mars where carbonates more available

raw.notes:
Complete ball bearing set production process for heavy machinery. Produces one set of
heavy-duty ball bearings suitable for high-load applications.

Process steps:
1. **Forging**: Upset forging to create inner and outer race ring blanks from bar stock
2. **Rough machining**: Turn races to near-final dimensions on lathe (raceways, shoulders, bore, OD)
3. **Heat treatment**:
   - Carburize or through-harden to HRC 58-62
   - Quench in oil
   - Temper at 150-200°C for dimensional stability and toughness
4. **Precision grinding**: Grind raceways to final tolerances (±0.005mm) and surface finish (Ra 0.2μm)
5. **Ball production**:
   - Cast or forge ball blanks
   - Rough grind to near-spherical
   - Heat treat to HRC 60-65
   - Precision lap/grind for sphericity and surface finish
6. **Cage fabrication**: Stamp or machine cage from steel sheet/bar
7. **Assembly**: Install balls in races with cage, pack with grease, seal
8. **Inspection**: Check running torque, radial play, and smoothness

Typical bearing specifications for "heavy" set (updated to realistic 4kg total):
- Bore: 70-100mm (size 6314-6320)
- OD: 130-180mm
- Width: 30-40mm
- Load rating: 100-200 kN dynamic
- ~12-16 balls per bearing
- Mass: ~2 kg per bearing
- Set includes: 2 bearings (one at each end of shaft)

Critical quality requirements:
- Hardness: HRC 58-65 for races and balls (wear resistance)
- Surface finish: Ra 0.1-0.4 μm (low friction, long life)
- Dimensional tolerance: ISO P6 or better (smooth running)
- Residual stress: Properly tempered (prevent cracking)

Material: High-carbon steel (0.95-1.10% C) or bearing steel equivalent (SAE 52100)

This is a simplified integrated process. In practice, bearing manufacturing is highly
specialized with dedicated machinery for each operation.

raw.notes:
Bosch reaction for reducing carbon dioxide to solid carbon using hydrogen.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: CO2 + 2H2 → C + 2H2O
Temperature: 530-730°C
Catalyst: Iron or nickel
Process: Catalytic reduction of CO2 to elemental carbon
Purpose: Regenerate carbon for FFC Cambridge graphite anodes
CO2 recycling in closed-loop ISRU systems
Products:
  - C (solid carbon): FFC anode material, reducing agent, feedstock
  - H2O (water): Electrolyzed to recycle H2 + generate O2
Water electrolysis: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
  - Hydrogen recycled back to Bosch reaction
  - Oxygen as valuable by-product
Net reaction with H2 recycling: CO2 → C + O2
Stoichiometry: CO2 (44g) + 2H2 (4g) → C (12g) + 2H2O (36g)
Mass fractions: 27.3% C, 81.8% H2O from inputs
Hydrogen source: Water electrolysis, volatile extraction
CO2 source: FFC process, life support, combustion
Catalyst considerations:
  - Iron: Abundant from ilmenite/meteorite processing
  - Nickel: From Mond process purification
  - Catalyst promotes carbon deposition on surface
Comparison to Sabatier reaction:
  - Sabatier: CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O (produces methane)
  - Bosch: CO2 + 2H2 → C + 2H2O (produces solid carbon)
  - Bosch uses less H2, directly produces carbon
Applications:
  - Carbon regeneration for FFC graphite anodes
  - CO2 removal from life support atmospheres
  - Carbon feedstock for chemical synthesis
Lunar ISRU: Critical for carbon cycle closure
Prevents depletion of scarce carbon volatiles
Coupled with water electrolysis for complete recycling
Alternative to Boudouard for carbon regeneration
Terrestrial use: Space station CO2 scrubbing (ISS uses Sabatier instead)

Boudouard reaction for converting carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide using carbon.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: C + CO2 → 2CO (endothermic)
Temperature: ~700°C (equilibrium shifts right with increasing temperature)
Process: Gas-solid heterogeneous reaction
Purpose: Regenerate CO for Mond/carbonyl metal purification processes
Convert waste CO2 back to useful CO
Close carbon cycle in FFC Cambridge process
Thermodynamics:
  - Endothermic (ΔH = +172 kJ/mol)
  - Favored at high temperature (Le Chatelier)
  - Reverse reaction (2CO → C + CO2) favored at low temp
Products:
  - CO (carbon monoxide): Mond process feedstock, reducing agent
Stoichiometry: C (12g) + CO2 (44g) → 2CO (56g)
Mass fractions: Input 21.4% C, 100% CO2 → Output 127% CO (from combined inputs)
Applications:
  - CO regeneration for Mond/carbonyl processes (Ni, Fe, Co, W purification)
  - Carbon cycle closure for FFC Cambridge anode consumption
  - Chemical feedstock production
Carbon source: FFC anode consumption, volatile extraction, pyrolysis
CO2 source: FFC process, combustion, respiration, fermentation
Reverse reaction (Boudouard equilibrium):
  - At <700°C: 2CO → C + CO2 (disproportionation)
  - Used to deposit carbon from CO
Industrial applications: Blast furnaces, gasification, synthesis gas
Lunar context: Essential for carbon recycling in closed-loop ISRU
Prevents carbon loss from system
Equilibrium depends on temperature - operate above 700°C for forward reaction
Can use solar thermal or resistive heating

raw.notes:
Production of calcium carbonate from calcium hydroxide via carbonation.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Reaction: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O (exothermic)
Temperature: Ambient to moderate (20-80°C)
Process: Gas-solid or gas-slurry carbonation
Purpose: CO2 capture and sequestration
Regenerate CaCO3 for Solvay process or CaO production
Utilize Ca(OH)2 by-product from HCl recovery
Process details:
  1. Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime) from CaCl2 hydrolysis or CaO hydration
  2. Bubble CO2 gas through Ca(OH)2 slurry
  3. CaCO3 (calcium carbonate/limestone) precipitates
  4. Filter and dry CaCO3 solid
  5. Water separated and recycled
Products:
  - CaCO3 (calcium carbonate): Solvay process input, calcination to CaO
  - H2O (water): Process water
Ca(OH)2 sources:
  - CaCl2 + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl (hydrolysis)
  - CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 (hydration)
CO2 sources:
  - FFC Cambridge process (anode consumption)
  - Solvay process (NaHCO3 calcination)
  - Life support systems (respiration)
  - Combustion, fermentation
CaCO3 applications:
  - Solvay process: 2NaCl + CaCO3 → Na2CO3 + CaCl2
  - Calcination: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (at 1000-1100°C)
  - Cement production: Component of Portland cement
  - CO2 sequestration: Stable mineral form
Stoichiometry: Ca(OH)2 (74g) + CO2 (44g) → CaCO3 (100g) + H2O (18g)
Mass fractions: 135% CaCO3, 24.3% H2O from Ca(OH)2 input
Calcium cycle:
  1. CaAl2Si2O8 (anorthite) → CaO (carbothermal)
  2. CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 (hydration)
  3. This process: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3
  4. CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (calcination to restart)
Advantages: Low temperature, low energy
Exothermic (releases heat)
CO2 capture and sequestration
Closes calcium cycle
Simple, well-understood chemistry
Disadvantages: Requires CO2 input
Slow kinetics (hours for completion)
Filtration/separation required
Lunar context: CO2 recycling critical (scarce carbon)
Ca(OH)2 from multiple process by-products
Enables CaCO3 regeneration for Solvay process
Potential for CO2 storage in stable mineral form
Part of integrated calcium-carbon recycling system

raw.notes:
Production of calcium chloride from calcium oxide and hydrochloric acid.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O (highly exothermic)
Temperature: Exothermic reaction (releases heat), then dry at 200-300°C
Process: Acid-base neutralization followed by dehydration
Purpose: Generate CaCl2 for FFC Cambridge electrolyte replenishment
Utilize CaO by-product from anorthite processing
Close chlorine recycling loop
Process details:
  1. CaO (quicklime) from anorthite carbothermal reduction
  2. React with HCl (from artificial weathering, recycled)
  3. Highly exothermic - temperature rises significantly
  4. CaCl2 solution forms, then dry to anhydrous salt
  5. Water condensed and separated

  - H2O (water): Process water, recyclable
CaO source: CaAl2Si2O8 + 4C → CaO + Al2O3 + 2Si + 4CO
HCl source: Recycled from anorthite leaching or other chlorine processes
FFC Cambridge electrolyte:
  - Molten CaCl2 bath at 900-1100°C
  - Losses from cathode porosity and handling (~10%)
  - This process replenishes lost electrolyte
Stoichiometry: CaO (56g) + 2HCl (73g) → CaCl2 (111g) + H2O (18g)
Mass fractions: 198% CaCl2 from CaO input
Advantages: Simple exothermic reaction
Utilizes waste CaO from preprocessing
Replenishes critical FFC electrolyte
HCl recycled (not consumed overall)
Disadvantages: Highly exothermic (requires careful control)
Drying step needed for anhydrous salt
Lunar context: CaO abundant from anorthite (70-95% of highlands)
Critical for maintaining FFC operations
Closes calcium-chlorine loop:
  CaAl2Si2O8 → CaO → CaCl2 (FFC) → repeat
Alternative use: Desiccant, road de-icing (Earth), dust control
Heat of reaction can be recovered for other processes
Essential process for FFC Cambridge sustainability

energy_model.notes: Roasting at 600°C plus Claus reaction at 750-1100°C

time_model.notes: Two-stage roasting and sulfur recovery

raw.notes:
Claus process for recovering elemental sulfur from troilite (iron sulfide).
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Stage 1 - Roasting: 4FeS + 7O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 4SO2 (at 600°C)
Stage 2 - Claus reaction: SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O (at 750-1100°C)
Catalyst: Alumina (Al2O3 from anorthite processing)
Process: Two-stage oxidation and reduction
Purpose: Extract elemental sulfur from meteoritic/regolith troilite
Sulfur used as catalyst in Mond/carbonyl processes
Process details:
  1. Troilite (FeS) from meteorites or lunar regolith (~1% in regolith)
  2. Stage 1: Roast in oxygen to produce Fe2O3 and SO2
  3. Stage 2: React SO2 with H2S over alumina catalyst
  4. Elemental sulfur (S) produced and collected (molten above 115°C)
  5. Fe2O3 (hematite) by-product for iron extraction
Products:
  - S (elemental sulfur): Catalyst for Mond process (CO + Ni → Ni(CO)4)
  - Fe2O3 (hematite): Iron ore for reduction to metal (modeled as iron_ore_or_ilmenite)
  - H2O (water): Process water
Troilite sources:
  - NiFe meteorites: Often associated with troilite inclusions
  - Lunar regolith: ~1% troilite content
  - Also with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and graphite
H2S source: Can be generated from troilite + acid, or recycle from process
Sulfur applications (critical):
  - Mond process catalyst: Ni + 4CO ⇌ Ni(CO)4 (requires S catalyst)
  - Similar for Fe, Co carbonyl processes
  - Chemical synthesis: Sulfuric acid, vulcanization (Earth)
Stoichiometry:
  - Roasting: 4FeS (352g) + 7O2 (224g) → 2Fe2O3 (320g) + 4SO2 (256g)
  - Claus: SO2 (64g) + 2H2S (68g) → 3S (96g) + 2H2O (36g)
  - Overall from FeS: FeS (88g) + O2 → Fe2O3 + S (with H2S input)
Mass fractions: 182% Fe2O3, 109% S from troilite input
Iron oxide reduction: Fe2O3 + 3H2 → 2Fe + 3H2O (hydrogen reduction)
Or: Fe2O3 + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO (carbothermal)
Advantages: Recovers valuable sulfur catalyst
Fe2O3 by-product useful for iron production
Proven industrial process (Claus widely used)
Alumina catalyst from abundant lunar anorthite
Disadvantages: Two-stage complexity
Requires H2S input (can recycle within process)
High temperatures for both stages
Troilite relatively scarce in bulk regolith
Lunar context: Sulfur critical catalyst for Mond process
Mond process essential for Ni/Fe/Co purification
Meteorite processing provides troilite + metals
Sulfur must be conserved (scarce resource)
Alternative sulfur source: Volcanic deposits (if accessible)
Troilite associated with impact craters and meteoritic material

raw.name: Cobalt extraction via sulfate route

energy_model.notes: Roasting, leaching, and electrowinning energy (per 1 kg feed batch)

time_model.notes: Roasting, leaching, and electrowinning sequence

raw.notes:
Cobalt purification via sulfate roasting and electrowinning route.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Process: Sulfate formation → aqueous leaching → electrolytic deposition
Temperature: 600-800°C for roasting, ambient for leaching, ambient for electrowinning
Purpose: Alternative to carbonyl process for cobalt purification
Useful when CO is scarce or sulfur is abundant
Process details:
  1. Impure cobalt metal (from meteoritic NiFe material)
  2. Roast with sulfur in oxygen atmosphere
  3. Reaction: 2Co + S + 2O2 → 2CoSO4 (cobalt sulfate)
  4. Alternative: Co + S → CoS, then 2CoS + 3O2 → 2CoSO4
  5. Cobalt sulfate is water-soluble
  6. Leach roasted material in water
  7. CoSO4 dissolves, impurities remain as residue
  8. Filter solution to remove insoluble impurities
  9. Electrowinning: Cathode: Co²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Co (pure metal)
  10. Anode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
  11. Pure cobalt metal deposits on cathode
Products:
  - Pure cobalt metal: 95% yield, >99% purity
  - Cobalt sulfate solution: Recycled or retained for other uses
  - Process water: Recycled
  - Oxygen: From electrowinning anode reaction
Stoichiometry:
  - Roasting: 2Co (118g) + S (32g) + 2O2 (64g) → 2CoSO4 (310g)
  - Leaching: CoSO4 + 7H2O → CoSO4·7H2O (soluble)
  - Electrowinning: Co²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Co
Roasting chemistry:
  - Direct sulfation: 2Co + S + 2O2 → 2CoSO4 (preferred)
  - Or two-stage: Co + S → CoS, then 2CoS + 3O2 → 2CoSO4
  - Temperature: 600-800°C (avoid Co3O4 formation)
  - Atmosphere: Excess oxygen ensures complete sulfation
Leaching chemistry:
  - CoSO4 very soluble in water (36.1g/100mL at 20°C)
  - Forms pink solution (Co²⁺ hydrated complex)
  - pH control important (slightly acidic, pH 4-6)
  - Impurities (Fe, Ni, Si) remain insoluble or precipitate
Electrowinning parameters:
  - Electrolyte: CoSO4 solution (100-150 g/L Co)
  - Anode: Inert (Pb, graphite, or dimensionally stable anode)
  - Cathode: Stainless steel or titanium starter sheet
  - Current density: 200-400 A/m²
  - Voltage: 2.5-3.5V
  - Temperature: 40-60°C (moderate heating improves kinetics)
Purity and yield:
  - Cobalt purity: >99% (high-purity from electrolytic deposition)
  - Yield: 95% (5% losses to solution, residues)
Applications of pure cobalt:
  - Superalloys: High-temperature turbine blades (Co-Cr-W)
  - Magnets: SmCo, AlNiCo permanent magnets
  - Catalysts: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, hydrogenation
  - Batteries: LiCoO2 cathodes (lithium-ion batteries)
  - Tool steel: Cobalt-tungsten high-speed steel
  - Hard facing: Wear-resistant coatings (stellite)
Advantages: Does not require CO (unlike carbonyl process)
  Water-based chemistry (simpler than gas-phase)
  High purity from electrowinning
  Sulfur can be recovered from troilite (FeS in meteorites)
  Scalable process
Disadvantages: Multi-step process (roasting, leaching, electrowinning)
  Requires sulfur input (consumable)
  Energy for roasting and electrolysis
  Aqueous processing requires water (recycled but needed)
Comparison to carbonyl process:
  - Carbonyl: Co + 4CO ⇌ Co2(CO)8 (gas) → Co (at 150°C, 35 bar)
  - Sulfate: Solid-liquid-electrochemical route
  - Carbonyl: Higher purity, lower temperature, requires CO
  - Sulfate: More robust, works with impure feed, requires sulfur
Lunar context: Cobalt extremely scarce (meteoritic only)
  Must extract from NiFe meteorite material with high efficiency
  Sulfur available from troilite (FeS) in meteorites
  Sulfate route viable if sulfur abundant locally
  Carbonyl route preferred if CO available (from FFC or Boudouard)
Sulfur recovery from troilite:
  - FeS + O2 → FeO + SO2 (or FeS roasting → Fe2O3 + SO2)
  - Claus process: SO2 + H2S → S + H2O
  - Sulfur for cobalt sulfate roasting
Impurity removal:
  - Iron: Precipitates as Fe(OH)3 at pH 4-6
  - Nickel: May co-extract; separate by selective precipitation
  - Copper: More noble, may co-deposit (use current control)
  - Silicon: Insoluble, removed in leaching residue
Process optimization:
  - Roasting: Optimize S:Co ratio (slight excess S)
  - Leaching: Multiple stages for maximum extraction
  - Electrowinning: Control current density to avoid dendritic growth
Solution recycling:
  - Spent electrolyte (depleted CoSO4) returned to leaching
  - Continuous process with solution recirculation
  - Make-up sulfuric acid as needed
Alternative precipitation route:
  - CoSO4 + 2NaOH → Co(OH)2 + Na2SO4
  - Co(OH)2 → CoO + H2O (at 200°C)
  - CoO + H2 → Co + H2O (hydrogen reduction)
  - Avoids electrowinning but requires H2
Cobalt hydroxide (intermediate):
  - Pink precipitate, Co(OH)2
  - Can be thermally decomposed to CoO (black)
  - CoO reduced to Co with H2 or C
Environmental considerations:
  - Cobalt sulfate toxic (handle with care)
  - Must contain all solutions (closed-loop processing)
  - Electrowinning produces O2 (useful by-product)

raw.name: Czochralski process for single-crystal silicon

energy_model.notes: High energy for melting ~1 kg silicon at 1600°C and precise temperature control

time_model.notes: Slow crystal pulling over 12-24 hours

raw.notes:
Czochralski (CZ) process for growing single-crystal silicon ingots.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Process: Seed crystal dipping and slow pulling from molten silicon
Temperature: ~1600°C (silicon melting point: 1414°C, kept just above)
Atmosphere: Vacuum or inert gas (argon) to prevent contamination
Purpose: Convert polysilicon to single-crystal silicon
Essential for electronics (integrated circuits, high-performance solar)
Process details:
  1. Charge fused silica crucible_refractory with polysilicon chunks
  2. Heat to 1600°C in vacuum or argon atmosphere
  3. Dip seed crystal (known orientation, e.g., <100> or <111>) into melt
  4. Slowly pull seed upward while rotating (1-10 mm/min)
  5. Silicon solidifies on seed in single-crystal form
  6. Control pull rate and temperature to control diameter
  7. Typical ingot: 200-300mm diameter, 1-2m length
  8. Cool ingot, remove from puller
Products:
  - Single-crystal silicon ingot (cylindrical boule)
  - Scrap polysilicon (cropped ends, re-melt)
Seed crystal:
  - Small single-crystal silicon rod (oriented)
  - Determines crystal orientation of entire ingot
  - Common orientations: <100> (electronics), <111> (some applications)
Crucible: Ceramic refractory (placeholder for fused silica or equivalent)
  - Slowly dissolves into melt (oxygen contamination source)
  - Replaced after each run or few runs
Dopant addition: Can add B (p-type) or P/As (n-type) during growth
Crystal quality:
  - Dislocation-free (or very low dislocation density)
  - Uniform crystal orientation throughout
  - Controlled resistivity via doping
Stoichiometry: Polysilicon → Single-crystal silicon (95% yield)
  - 5% losses from cropping, surface defects
Advantages: Produces large, high-quality single crystals
Well-controlled process (diameter, doping, orientation)
Standard for semiconductor industry
Suitable for high-efficiency solar cells (>25%)
Disadvantages: Energy intensive (80-100 kWh/kg)
Slow process (12-24 hours per ingot)
Requires ultra-pure polysilicon input
Crucible consumption (SiO2)
5% material loss
Applications:
  - Electronics: Wafers → integrated circuits, processors, memory
  - Solar cells: High-efficiency monocrystalline panels
  - Sensors: MEMS, photodetectors, pressure sensors
  - Power devices: Rectifiers, thyristors, MOSFETs
Post-processing: Ingot → sliced into wafers → polished → device fabrication
Lunar/space context: Essential for in-situ electronics manufacturing
Enables computational infrastructure
High-efficiency solar power generation
Sensors for robotic systems
Alternative: Float-zone (FZ) process for higher purity, smaller diameter

entities.name: Direct FFC reduction of anorthite to AlCaSi alloy

raw.name: Direct FFC reduction of anorthite to AlCaSi alloy

energy_model.notes: FFC electrolysis at 900-1100°C for complex oxide (1 kg batch)

time_model.notes: Direct reduction of feldspar to alloy sponge

raw.notes:
Direct FFC Cambridge reduction of anorthite to produce AlCaSi mongrel alloy.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, ellery-et-al-2022-metalysis
Reaction: CaAl2Si2O8 → AlCaSi alloy + O2 (via electrolysis in CaCl2)
Temperature: 900-1100°C (molten CaCl2 electrolyte)
Voltage: 2.5-3V typical
Process: Direct electrolytic reduction without preprocessing
Purpose: Simple one-step alloy production from abundant anorthite
Highland regolith is 70-95% anorthite-rich anorthosite
Structural material and specialty applications
Process details:
  1. Anorthite ore (CaAl2Si2O8) from highland regolith
  2. Powder, compact, and sinter into cathode form
  3. Immerse in molten CaCl2 electrolyte at 900-1100°C
  4. Apply voltage (graphite anode)
  5. AlCaSi alloy forms as porous metallic sponge
  6. Oxygen released at anode (with C → CO/CO2)
  7. Remove alloy sponge, densify or remelt
Products:
  - AlCaSi alloy: Aluminum-calcium-silicon mongrel alloy
  - O2 (oxygen): Valuable by-product (46% by mass!)
Alloy composition (theoretical from CaAl2Si2O8):
  - Al: 19.4% by mass (from Al2O3 component)
  - Ca: 14.4% (from CaO component)
  - Si: 20.2% (from 2 SiO2 components)
  - Total metal: 54.0% of anorthite mass
Actual alloy properties: NEED INVESTIGATION
  - AlSi alloys are well-known (silumin: casting alloys)
  - AlCa: Less common, Ca additions improve castability
  - AlCaSi: Ternary alloy, properties not well-characterized
Potential applications:
  - Casting alloy: AlSi (20-50% Si) used for high-fluidity castings
  - Brazing filler metal: AlSi used for joining aluminum parts
  - Structural material: Moderate strength, low density
  - Wear-resistant surfaces: Si precipitates provide hardness
AlSi alloy benefits (from terrestrial use):
  - Lower viscosity than pure Al (better casting)
  - Low thermal expansion
  - Good wear resistance (Si particles)
  - Etching can create porous Si for oil retention (engine applications)
Stoichiometry: CaAl2Si2O8 (278.2g) → Ca (40.1g) + 2Al (54g) + 2Si (56.2g) + 4 O2 (128g)
Total metals: 150.3g (54.0%), oxygen: 46.0%
Advantages: Single-step process from most abundant lunar mineral
  Anorthite is 70-95% of highlands (vast resource)
  Very high oxygen yield (46% by mass!)
  No preprocessing required
  Potentially useful alloy properties
Disadvantages: "Mongrel" composition not precisely controlled
  Ca inclusion may or may not be beneficial
  Properties unknown - requires testing
  Not suitable for applications requiring pure Al or Si
Comparison to pure metal routes:
  - Pure: CaAl2Si2O8 + 4C → CaO + Al2O3 + 2Si (carbothermal), then separate
  - Or: HCl leaching → CaCl2 + Al2O3 + SiO2, then FFC each separately
  - Mongrel: Direct FFC (simplest but least controlled)
Lunar context: Anorthite THE most abundant highland mineral
  This route exploits highlands abundance directly
  Suitable for bulk structural material
  Trade simplicity for material property uncertainty
Oxygen yield exceptional: 46% by mass from anorthite!
  Higher than any other lunar mineral process
  Critical for life support and propellant
Iron contamination tolerance:
  - Highland anorthite has low Fe (<1%)
  - Can add Ni, Co from meteorite sources to strengthen
Next steps: Metallurgical characterization of AlCaSi alloy
  Tensile strength, hardness, corrosion resistance
  Casting properties, weldability
  May be suitable for many applications as-is
  Or further processing to separate components

raw.name: FFC Cambridge calcium metal extraction

energy_model.notes: Electrolysis at 900-1100°C, lower than Hall-Heroult

time_model.notes: FFC reduction of CaO to calcium metal

raw.notes:
FFC Cambridge process for extracting pure calcium metal from calcium oxide.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Cathode reaction: CaO + 2e⁻ → Ca + O²⁻
Anode reaction: C + O²⁻ → CO + 2e⁻ (or C + 2O²⁻ → CO2 + 4e⁻)
Overall: CaO → Ca + ½O2 (with C anode: CaO + C → Ca + CO/CO2)
Temperature: 900-1100°C in molten CaCl2 electrolyte
Voltage: 2.5-3V typical
Products: High-purity calcium metal (>99%), oxygen gas
Calcium oxide source: Anorthite carbothermal reduction, lime calcination
Calcium metal properties:
  - More conductive by mass than copper (low density)
  - Melting point: 842°C (tapped as liquid above this)
  - Density: 1.55 g/cm³
  - Electrical conductor for vacuum applications
  - Chemical reactant for Pidgeon process (Mg extraction)
CaCl2 electrolyte recycled (losses <10%)
Carbon anode consumed, CO/CO2 can be recycled via Bosch/Boudouard
FFC process operates in solid state until Ca melts
Stoichiometry: CaO (56.1 g/mol) → Ca (40.1g) + 0.5 O2 (16g)

raw.notes:
Direct FFC Cambridge reduction of ilmenite to produce ferrotitanium mongrel alloy.
Source: ellery-et-al-2022-metalysis-fray-farthing-chen-process, FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt
Reaction: FeTiO3 → FeTi alloy + O2 (via electrolysis in CaCl2)
Temperature: 900-1100°C (molten CaCl2 electrolyte)
Voltage: 2.5-3V typical
Process: Direct electrolytic reduction without preprocessing
Purpose: Simple one-step alloy production from ilmenite
Alternative to hydrogen reduction + separation
Structural material and specialty applications
Process details:
  1. Ilmenite concentrate (FeTiO3) from mare regolith
  2. Sinter into cathode pellet/rod
  3. Immerse in molten CaCl2 electrolyte at 900-1100°C
  4. Apply voltage (graphite anode)
  5. FeTi alloy forms as porous sponge at cathode
  6. Oxygen released at anode (CO/CO2 with graphite)
  7. Remove alloy sponge, mechanically densify or remelt
Products:
  - FeTi alloy (ferrotitanium): 45-75% Ti typical composition
  - O2 (oxygen): Valuable by-product
Ferrotitanium alloy applications:
  - General structural material (moderate strength)
  - Oxygen scavenging in metallurgy (deoxidation agent)
  - Pyrotechnic fuel (reacts vigorously with O2)
  - Specialty alloy additive
Alloy composition:
  - Depends on exact ilmenite composition
  - FeTiO3 theoretically → ~52% Ti, 48% Fe by mass
  - Actual: 45-75% Ti range (ferroti tanium specification)
Stoichiometry: FeTiO3 (151.7g) → Fe (55.8g) + Ti (47.9g) + 1.5 O2 (48g)
Total metal: 103.7g (68.3% of ilmenite), oxygen: 31.6%
Advantages: Single-step process (no preprocessing)
  Simpler than H2 reduction + Fe/TiO2 separation
  Alloy suitable for many applications as-is
  Higher oxygen yield than H2 reduction
  Well-suited for bulk structural material production
Disadvantages: "Mongrel" alloy composition not precisely controlled
  Properties need investigation
  Not suitable where pure Fe or pure Ti required
  Oxygen-scavenging property may limit applications
  (reacts with free O2 - problematic in oxidizing environments)
Comparison to pure metal routes:
  - Pure route: FeTiO3 + H2 → Fe + TiO2, then separate and purify
  - Mongrel route: FeTiO3 → FeTi alloy directly (simpler)
Lunar context: Ilmenite abundant in mare basalts (10-25% by weight)
  Simplest route for structural metal from ilmenite
  Suitable for non-critical structures, tools, equipment
  Trade-off: Simplicity vs. material property control
Oxygen yield: 31.6% by mass (good for ISRU)
Further processing: Can remelt alloy to densify
  Can add other elements to adjust properties
  Or separate Fe/Ti via subsequent processing if needed
Caution: Oxygen-scavenging property
  - FeTi + O2 → oxides (exothermic, pyrotechnic)
  - Should not be used where free O2 present
  - Suitable for vacuum or inert atmosphere applications
  - Or as deoxidizer in metallurgy (intentional use)

raw.notes:
Direct FFC Cambridge reduction of olivine to produce MgSi mongrel alloy.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt
Reaction: Mg2SiO4 → MgSi alloy + O2 (via electrolysis in CaCl2)
Temperature: 900-1100°C (molten CaCl2 electrolyte)
Voltage: 2.5-3V typical
Process: Direct electrolytic reduction without preprocessing
Purpose: Simple one-step alloy production from crater olivine deposits
Alloying additive and specialty applications
Process details:
  1. Olivine ore (Mg2SiO4 forsterite or Fe2SiO4 fayalite)
  2. Powder, compact, and sinter into cathode pellet
  3. Immerse in molten CaCl2 electrolyte at 900-1100°C
  4. Apply voltage (graphite anode)
  5. MgSi alloy (or MgFeSi for fayalite) forms at cathode
  6. Oxygen released at anode (CO/CO2 with graphite)
  7. Remove alloy sponge, process as needed
Products:
  - MgSi alloy: Magnesium-silicon alloy
  - O2 (oxygen): High yield (45.5% by mass)
Alloy composition (from forsterite Mg2SiO4):
  - Mg: 34.5% by mass
  - Si: 19.9% by mass
  - Total metal: 54.5% of olivine mass
For fayalite (Fe2SiO4):
  - Fe: 49.2%, Si: 19.9%, total: 69.1%
Mg2Si compound:
  - Intermetallic compound, not mechanical mixture
  - Used as strengthening agent in aluminum alloys
  - Improves strength, hardness, creep resistance
Applications:
  - Aluminum alloying: Small Mg2Si additions strengthen Al
  - Thermoelectric materials: Mg2Si has thermoelectric properties
  - Semiconductor: Mg2Si is narrow-gap semiconductor
  - Pyrotechnic fuel: Mg + Si + oxidizer (ground into powder)
  - Hydrogen storage: Mg2Si can absorb/release H2
Stoichiometry: Mg2SiO4 (140.7g) → 2Mg (48.6g) + Si (28.1g) + 2 O2 (64g)
Total metals: 76.7g (54.5%), oxygen: 45.5%
Fe contamination tolerance:
  - Most lunar olivine is mixed Mg-Fe composition
  - FeTiO3 olivine → MgFeSi alloy
  - Fe may or may not be problematic depending on use
Advantages: Direct single-step process
  High oxygen yield (45.5%)
  Olivine common in crater ejecta and some maria
  Mg2Si useful as Al alloy additive
  Multiple potential applications
Disadvantages: "Mongrel" alloy with uncertain properties
  Olivine less abundant than anorthite or ilmenite
  Mg vacuum outgassing concern (though in alloy form)
  Composition varies with olivine Mg/Fe ratio
  Not suitable for pure Mg or pure Si applications
Comparison to pure metal routes:
  - Pidgeon: Mg2SiO4 + 2CaO → 2Mg + Ca2SiO4 (pure Mg vapor)
  - Carbothermal: Mg2SiO4 + 2C → 2Mg + SiO + 2CO (pure components)
  - FFC pure: Separate MgO and SiO2, then FFC each
  - FFC mongrel: Direct (simplest but mixed alloy)
Lunar context: Olivine in crater regions and some maria
  Not as abundant as anorthite or ilmenite
  Suitable for specialty applications
  Mg2Si valuable for Al alloy strengthening
Magnesium concerns:
  - Mg outgasses in vacuum (vapor pressure)
  - Problematic for structural use in vacuum
  - Better suited for enclosed environments
  - Or alloying additions where Mg is minority component
Iron-bearing olivine (fayalite):
  - More common than pure forsterite
  - Fe2SiO4 → FeSi alloy + O2 (iron silicide)
  - May be more useful due to Fe inclusion
Potential: Investigate MgSi and MgFeSi alloy properties
  Mechanical strength, stability in vacuum
  Thermoelectric performance
  Hydrogen storage capacity
  Applications in lunar context

raw.name: HCl generation from NaCl using nitric acid

energy_model.notes: Moderate heating for HCl gas evolution (1 kg NaCl batch)

time_model.notes: Acid displacement reaction time

raw.notes:
Generation of hydrochloric acid gas from sodium chloride using nitric acid.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Reaction: NaCl + HNO3 → HCl + NaNO3
Temperature: Moderate heating (80-160°C for HCl gas evolution)
Process: Acid displacement - stronger acid displaces weaker from salt
Purpose: Generate HCl for artificial weathering and chlorine chemistry
Critical enabler for NaCl-based reagent recycling
Process details:
  1. NaCl (solid salt, imported from Earth as recycled reagent)
  2. React with HNO3 (from Ostwald process)
  3. HCl gas evolved, collected by condensation or absorption
  4. NaNO3 (sodium nitrate/saltpetre) remains as solid
Products:
  - HCl (hydrochloric acid gas): Artificial weathering, chlorine source
  - NaNO3 (sodium nitrate/saltpetre): Oxidizer, nitrogen storage
HCl applications (critical):
  - Anorthite leaching: CaAl2Si2O8 + 8HCl → products (recycled HCl)
  - Carbochlorination: Provides Cl2 source
  - Silicon purification: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 (recycled HCl)
  - Rochow process: Forms CH3Cl for silicone synthesis
  - All processes recycle HCl - not consumed
NaCl recycling chain:
  1. NaCl (import) + HNO3 → HCl + NaNO3
  2. HCl used in processes, regenerated
  3. NaNO3 + KCl → NaCl + KNO3 (recovers NaCl)
  - KCl from orthoclase processing
Stoichiometry: NaCl (58.5g) + HNO3 (63g) → HCl (36.5g) + NaNO3 (85g)
Mass fractions: 62.4% HCl, 145% NaNO3 from NaCl input
Nitric acid source: Ostwald process from ammonia
Nitrogen conservation: NaNO3 stores nitrogen as saltpetre
Advantages: Simple acid-base chemistry
Enables all chlorine chemistry from single NaCl import
HCl recycled through all downstream processes
NaNO3 useful as oxidizer and N storage
Disadvantages: Requires scarce nitrogen (via HNO3)
NaCl must be imported from Earth (scarce on Moon)
Multi-step process to establish reagents

raw.notes:
Recovery of hydrochloric acid from calcium chloride via high-temperature hydrolysis.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Reaction: CaCl2 + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl (above 425°C)
Temperature: >425°C (high temperature required for reaction)
Process: Steam hydrolysis to regenerate HCl
Purpose: Recover HCl from waste/spent CaCl2
Close hydrochloric acid recycling loop
Alternative to HCl generation from NaCl
Process details:
  1. CaCl2 (from Solvay by-product or other sources)
  2. High-temperature steam (H2O vapor above 425°C)
  3. Hydrolysis produces HCl gas and Ca(OH)2 solid
  4. HCl gas collected by condensation
  5. Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime) as solid by-product
Products:
  - HCl (hydrochloric acid gas): Recycled for artificial weathering
  - Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime): Cement component, CO2 capture
Calcium hydroxide applications:
  - Cement production: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O (carbonation)
  - Water treatment: pH adjustment
  - CO2 capture: Forms calcium carbonate
Stoichiometry: CaCl2 (111g) + 2H2O (36g) → Ca(OH)2 (74g) + 2HCl (73g)
Mass fractions: 66.7% Ca(OH)2, 65.7% HCl from CaCl2 input
HCl recycling chain:
  1. HCl used in processes (e.g., anorthite leaching)
  2. Regenerated in leaching: CaAl2Si2O8 + HCl → CaCl2 + ...
  3. This process: CaCl2 + H2O → HCl + Ca(OH)2
  4. HCl recycled to step 1
Advantages: Recovers HCl from spent CaCl2
Ca(OH)2 useful for cement and CO2 capture
Closes HCl recycling loop
Reduces reliance on NaCl import for HCl generation
Disadvantages: High temperature requirement (>425°C)
Additional processing step
Not all CaCl2 should be hydrolyzed (need for FFC electrolyte)
Lunar context: Enables true HCl recycling
CaCl2 from Solvay process can be split:
  - Portion to FFC electrolyte
  - Portion hydrolyzed to recover HCl
Ca(OH)2 useful for cement (habitat construction)
Alternative to constant NaCl consumption
Balance: Need both FFC electrolyte AND HCl recycling
Optimization required based on system demands

raw.notes:
Cryogenic separation of helium-3 from helium-4 for potential fusion fuel.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt
Process: Extreme cryogenic fractional distillation
Temperature: <4.2 K (near absolute zero, -269°C)
3He concentration: 4-30 ppb in regolith (parts per billion)
Purpose: Separate valuable 3He isotope for future nuclear fusion
3He extraction released with other volatiles (thermal processing)
Process details:
  1. Mixed He isotopes from regolith volatile extraction
  2. Cool to <4.2 K (He boiling point for 4He)
  3. Fractional distillation exploits boiling point difference:
     - 3He boiling point: 3.19 K
     - 4He boiling point: 4.22 K
     - ΔT = 1.03 K difference
  4. Multiple distillation stages for separation
  5. Collect 3He fraction (earlier to boil/condense)
  6. 4He remains as bulk fraction
  7. Store 3He in extreme cryogenic vessels (<4 K)
Products:
  - 3He (helium-3): Potential nuclear fusion fuel
  - 4He (helium-4): Inert gas, leak detection, cryogenic applications
3He concentration in regolith:
  - Average: 4 ppb (parts per billion)
  - High-Ti mare: Up to 10-30 ppb (mature regolith)
  - Mare Tranquillitatis, Oceanus Procellarum highest
  - Total lunar inventory: ~2 × 10⁸ kg (200 million kg)
Collection requirements:
  - 40 m² at 1m depth → 1g 3He (plus 8.2 kg carbon)
  - 40 km² at 1m depth → 1 metric tonne 3He
  - Massive scale required for significant quantities
3He nuclear fusion:
  - Reaction: D + 3He → 4He + p + 18.4 MeV (deuterium-helium-3)
  - Advantages: Aneutronic (no neutron radiation)
  - Less radioactive waste than D-T fusion
  - Disadvantages: Higher ignition temperature than D-T
  - D-T fusion not yet commercial, D-3He even further away
Stoichiometry: 1 kg mixed He → 14 μg 3He, 999.986 mg 4He (at 14 ppb)
At mature high-Ti mare (30 ppb): ~30 μg 3He per kg He
4He applications:
  - Inert atmosphere for welding, crystal growth
  - Leak detection (small molecule, easily detected)
  - Cryogenic applications (superfluid helium)
  - Balloon/airship gas (Earth applications)
Advantages: 3He extremely valuable for future fusion
  Released automatically with volatile extraction
  Separation technology well-established (terrestrial)
  4He by-product also useful
Disadvantages: Extremely low concentration (ppb level)
  Requires cryogenic storage at <4 K (challenging)
  Nuclear fusion still not commercially viable
  D-3He fusion even more difficult than D-T
  Massive processing required for useful quantities
Lunar context: 3He touted as "lunar resource" for future
  But fusion technology very far from reality
  Should 3He be husbanded for future generations?
  Or consumed/lost during volatile processing?
  Ethical question: Waste vs. extreme cryogenic storage
Storage requirements: <4 K cryogenic for indefinite storage
  - Extreme energy cost for refrigeration
  - Boil-off losses without perfect insulation
  - May not be practical for long-term lunar storage
Recommendation (per source papers): Capture and store if feasible
  But don't let 3He recovery block volatile extraction
  Volatiles (C, N, H) more immediately critical
  3He as bonus/future resource, not primary driver

energy_model.notes: Direct synthesis at 300-450°C, exothermic reaction

raw.notes:
Direct synthesis of hydrogen sulfide gas from hydrogen and elemental sulfur.
Reaction: H2 + S → H2S (exothermic)
Temperature: 300-450°C for controlled reaction rate
Process: Direct combination in reactor
Purpose: Produce H2S for Claus process sulfur recovery
Alternative: H2S can also be generated from troilite (FeS) + acid treatment
Process details:
  1. Elemental sulfur (from Claus process or sulfide ores)
  2. Hydrogen gas (from water electrolysis or regolith volatiles)
  3. Heat to 300-450°C in reactor
  4. Direct combination: H2 + S → H2S
  5. Exothermic reaction (releases ~20 kJ/mol)
  6. Cool and collect H2S gas
Products:
  - H2S (hydrogen sulfide): Used in Claus process (SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O)
Stoichiometry: H2 (2g) + S (32g) → H2S (34g)
Mass fractions: 5.9% H2, 94.1% S (matches H2S composition)
Advantages: Simple direct synthesis
  Enables sulfur recycling loop with Claus process
  Exothermic (releases heat)
Disadvantages: Produces toxic, corrosive gas
  Requires careful containment and handling
  Safety systems essential (scrubbers, monitors)
Lunar context: Enables closed-loop sulfur recovery
  H2S intermediate in Claus process
  Sulfur conserved (scarce lunar resource)
Safety: H2S extremely toxic (>10 ppm hazardous)
  Corrosive to metals
  Requires gas-tight reactor and scrubbing system
  Emergency shutdown and ventilation systems
Alternative H2S sources:
  - Troilite + HCl: FeS + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2S
  - Sulfide ore roasting off-gases
Sulfur recycling loop:
  1. Troilite roasting → SO2
  2. H2 + S → H2S (this process)
  3. SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O (Claus process)
  4. Sulfur recovered and recycled

Sulfuric acid leaching of ilmenite to extract iron and titanium as sulfates.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Primary reaction: FeTiO3 + 2H2SO4 → FeSO4 + TiOSO4 + 2H2O
Temperature: Elevated (80-150°C for concentrated H2SO4)
Process: Acid digestion in corrosion-resistant reactor
Products: Iron sulfate (FeSO4) and titanyl sulfate (TiOSO4) in solution
Requires downstream processing:
  1. FeSO4 + H2O → Fe + ½O2 + H2SO4 (electrolysis, acid recycled)
  2. TiOSO4 + H2O → H2SO4 + TiO2 (hydrolysis, acid recycled)
Advantages: Lower temperature than thermal routes, acid fully recycled
Disadvantages: Requires corrosive acid handling, multi-step process
Acid recycling essential - cannot consume sulfuric acid
Sulfur source: Lunar volatiles or troilite (FeS) from meteorites/regolith
Net products: Iron metal, titanium dioxide, oxygen gas
Stoichiometry: FeTiO3 (151.7g) + 2H2SO4 (196g) → FeSO4 (151.9g) + TiOSO4 (159.9g) + 2H2O (36g)
This process file represents only the leaching step
See companion processes for FeSO4 electrolysis and TiOSO4 hydrolysis
Complex but proven industrial route (used terrestrially)

raw.name: Methanol synthesis from syngas

energy_model.notes: Exothermic reaction at 250°C with pressure

time_model.notes: Catalytic synthesis and condensation

raw.notes:
Methanol synthesis from carbon monoxide and hydrogen (syngas).
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: CO + 2H2 → CH3OH (exothermic)
Temperature: 250°C
Pressure: 5-10 MPa (50-100 bar)
Catalyst: Alumina (Al2O3 from anorthite processing)
Process: Catalytic synthesis under pressure
Purpose: Second step in silicone plastic synthesis chain
Chemical feedstock for methyl chloride production
Industrial solvent and fuel
Process details:
  1. Syngas (CO + H2) from steam reforming
  2. Compressed to 5-10 MPa
  3. Passed over alumina catalyst at 250°C
  4. Methanol (CH3OH) produced
  5. Condense liquid methanol
  6. Unreacted syngas recycled
Products:
  - CH3OH (methanol/methyl alcohol): Feedstock for silicone synthesis
Alumina catalyst source:
  - Anorthite processing: CaAl2Si2O8 → Al2O3
  - HCl leaching: CaAl2Si2O8 + 8HCl → Al2O3 + ...
  - Carbothermal: CaAl2Si2O8 + 4C → Al2O3 + ...
Alcohol determination:
  - Methanol from methanol (CH3OH yields polydimethylsiloxane PDMS)
  - Higher alcohols yield different siloxanes
Next step: CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + H2O (methyl chloride for Rochow process)
Stoichiometry: CO (28g) + 2H2 (4g) → CH3OH (32g)
Mass fractions: 114% CH3OH from CO input
Syngas ratio: CO:H2 = 1:2 required (steam reforming gives 1:3, adjust)
Advantages: Exothermic reaction (releases heat)
High conversion efficiency (>90%)
Proven industrial process
Alumina catalyst from abundant lunar anorthite
Moderate temperature (vs steam reforming)
Disadvantages: High pressure requirement (5-10 MPa)
Equilibrium-limited (requires recycle of unreacted syngas)
Catalyst poisoning by sulfur and chlorides
Applications:
  - Silicone synthesis: → methyl chloride → dimethyldichlorosilane → PDMS
  - Chemical feedstock: Formaldehyde, acetic acid, MTBE
  - Fuel: Methanol fuel cells, combustion engines
  - Solvent: Industrial processes
Lunar context: Critical intermediate for silicone plastics
Silicone essential for: Wire insulation, seals, elastomers, gaskets
Limited alternatives to silicone for flexible electrical insulation
Methanol also useful as solvent for chemical processing
Alternative alcohols (ethanol, etc.) require different synthesis routes
Silicone chain: CH4 → syngas → CH3OH → CH3Cl → (CH3)2SiCl2 → PDMS

raw.name: Microwave sintering of regolith

energy_model.notes: Microwave heating couples efficiently with nanophase iron in regolith. Reaches 1000-1500°C with rapid heating (1000°C/min). More energy-efficient than conventional sintering due to volumetric heating and strong coupling with iron particles.

time_model.notes: Very rapid process due to efficient microwave coupling. 1000°C/min heating rate possible. Typical cycle: mold filling, microwave exposure (minutes), cooling. Can be performed in-situ with mobile microwave head on rover.

raw.notes:
Microwave sintering process for consolidating lunar regolith into solid construction blocks or in-situ structures.
Exploits the ubiquitous nanophase iron (np-Fe0) in lunar regolith which couples strongly with microwave radiation at 2.45 GHz.

Process characteristics:
- Operating temperature: 1000-1500°C (typically 1200°C, just below regolith melting point)
- Heating rate: Up to 1000°C/min due to excellent microwave coupling
- Compressive strength: 55 MPa achieved for microwave-sintered regolith bricks
- Stronger binding than solar sintering methods
- Can be performed in-situ using mobile microwave applicator head mounted on rover
- Typical microwave frequency: 2.45 GHz
- Power requirement: 100-350W (specification for equipment design)

Applications:
- Construction bricks and blocks
- Landing pad surfacing (in-situ sintering)
- Road/walkway paving
- Protective shells and structures
- Foundation pads for equipment

Sources:
- Ellery 2021 (Leveraging In-Situ Resources for Lunar Base Construction)
- Sustainable ISRU on the Moon
- Self-Replicating Machines on the Moon

Provenance: ai_estimate for energy/time values based on literature descriptions
Confidence: medium (process well-documented in literature, but exact parameters estimated)

Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Reaction: NaNO3 + KCl → NaCl + KNO3 (double displacement/metathesis)
Temperature: Moderate (100-200°C for crystallization)
Process: Ion exchange via differential solubility
Purpose: Regenerate NaCl from NaNO3 (HCl generation by-product)
Close sodium chloride recycling loop
Conserve imported NaCl reagent
Process details:
  1. NaNO3 (from NaCl + HNO3 → HCl + NaNO3 reaction)
  2. React with KCl (from orthoclase feldspar processing)
  3. Double displacement reaction
  4. Crystallization exploits different solubilities
  5. Separate NaCl and KNO3 by fractional crystallization
Products:
  - NaCl (sodium chloride): Recycled for HCl generation, Solvay process
  - KNO3 (potassium nitrate/saltpetre): Catalyst, oxidizer, N storage
KCl source: Orthoclase feldspar (KAlSi3O8)
  - Found in lunar KREEP regions (~8-18 mg/g K)
  - Processing similar to anorthite routes
KNO3 (saltpetre) applications:
  - Catalyst for selenium extraction: FeSe + Na2CO3 + O2 → Se (KNO3 catalyst)
  - Nitrogen storage form (more stable than NH3)
  - Oxidizer for pyrotechnics/propellants
  - Fertilizer (Earth/Mars agriculture)
Stoichiometry: NaNO3 (85g) + KCl (74.5g) → NaCl (58.5g) + KNO3 (101g)
Mass fractions: 68.8% NaCl, 119% KNO3 from NaNO3 input
Solubility exploitation:
  - Different salts have different temperature-dependent solubilities
  - Fractional crystallization separates products
NaCl recycling chain:
  1. NaCl (import) + HNO3 → HCl + NaNO3
  2. HCl used and recycled in various processes
  3. This process: NaNO3 + KCl → NaCl + KNO3
  4. NaCl returned to step 1
Advantages: Closes NaCl recycling loop
KCl from lunar orthoclase (KREEP regions)
KNO3 product useful as catalyst and N storage
Simple metathesis chemistry
Disadvantages: Requires KCl (less abundant than Na)
Fractional crystallization complexity
Not 100% efficiency (some losses)
Lunar context: Critical for NaCl conservation
Imported NaCl can be recycled indefinitely
KCl from KREEP processing unlocks this route
Nitrogen husbandry: NaNO3 → KNO3 → stored safely
Enables sustainable chlorine chemistry with minimal import

raw.notes:
Noble gas extraction (Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) from lunar regolith volatiles.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Purpose: Extract noble gases for ion engine propellant, inert atmospheres, and specialized uses
Concentration: <1 ppm total (highly rarefied)
WARNING: Extremely low concentrations - not practical for first-generation ISRU
Process details:
  1. Collect mixed volatiles from thermal regolith processing (700-1200°C)
  2. Remove reactive gases (CO2, H2O, N2) via chemical scrubbing
  3. Cool remaining gas mixture to cryogenic temperatures
  4. Multi-stage fractional distillation using boiling point differences:
     - Ne: 27.1 K (-246°C) boiling point
     - Ar: 87.3 K (-186°C)
     - Kr: 119.9 K (-153°C)
     - Xe: 165.1 K (-108°C)
  5. Sequential condensation and vaporization stages
  6. Collect purified noble gas fractions
  7. Store in high-pressure cylinders (compressed gas)
Products:
  - Neon (Ne): ~0.15 ppm (0.000015%) - inert atmosphere, cryogenics
  - Argon (Ar): ~0.5 ppm (0.00005%) - inert atmosphere, ion engines
  - Krypton (Kr): ~0.02 ppm - specialized lighting, ion engines
  - Xenon (Xe): ~0.003 ppm - ion engines, anesthesia, lighting
  - Other volatiles: He, H2, N2, CO, CH4 (separated earlier)
Concentration in regolith volatiles:
  - Ne: 0.1-0.3 ppm (parts per million)
  - Ar: 0.3-0.8 ppm
  - Kr: 0.01-0.03 ppm
  - Xe: 0.002-0.005 ppm
  - Total noble gases: <1 ppm (extremely rare)
Boiling points for separation:
  - He: 4.2 K (separated first, see helium-3 process)
  - Ne: 27.1 K
  - H2: 20.3 K (interferes with Ne, remove via chemical reaction)
  - N2: 77.4 K
  - Ar: 87.3 K
  - O2: 90.2 K (if present)
  - Kr: 119.9 K
  - Xe: 165.1 K
  - CO2: 194.7 K (sublimes, removed earlier)
Separation strategy:
  1. Remove CO2 (194K): Sublimation or chemical scrubbing
  2. Liquefy Xe (165K): Condense, remove
  3. Liquefy Kr (120K): Condense, remove
  4. Liquefy Ar (87K): Condense, remove (with N2)
  5. Separate Ar from N2: Additional distillation (7K difference)
  6. Liquefy Ne (27K): Condense, remove (separate from H2)
  7. He remains gaseous (4K for liquefaction)
Applications:
  - Xenon ion engines: High Isp (3000-5000 s), efficient propulsion
    - Xe: Heavy atom (131 amu), easily ionized (12.1 eV)
    - Best ion engine propellant (NSTAR, NEXT, HiPEP)
  - Krypton ion engines: Alternative to Xe, lighter (84 amu)
  - Argon: Inert atmosphere for welding, crystal growth
    - Arc welding (TIG/MIG): Prevents oxidation
    - FFC Cambridge: Inert environment (alternative to vacuum)
  - Neon: Cryogenic refrigerant, lighting (neon signs)
  - All: Leak detection, inert gas purging
Advantages: Noble gases valuable for propulsion (ion engines)
  Released automatically with volatile extraction
  No chemical processing needed (inert, don't react)
  Can be stored indefinitely (stable)
Disadvantages: Extremely low concentration (<1 ppm)
  Requires processing huge quantities of regolith
  Energy-intensive cryogenic separation
  Not economical for early ISRU
Lunar context: Noble gases implanted by solar wind
  Concentration depends on regolith maturity and exposure
  Mare regolith typically higher than highland
  Mature regolith (billion years exposure) highest
Scale requirements (example for Xe):
  - Xe concentration: ~3 ppb (0.000003%)
  - For 1 kg Xe: Must process ~330,000 kg regolith volatiles
  - Regolith volatile content: ~0.01% by mass
  - Total regolith: ~33 million kg (33,000 tonnes!)
  - Clearly not practical for small-scale ISRU
Ion engine propellant requirements:
  - Typical ion engine: 5-10 mg/s Xe consumption
  - 1 kg Xe: 100,000-200,000 seconds runtime (~28-56 hours)
  - Deep space missions: 100s-1000s kg Xe required
  - Lunar extraction cannot supply mission-scale quantities
Energy analysis:
  - Regolith heating: ~0.5 kWh/kg regolith
  - Cryogenic refrigeration: ~50 kWh/kg noble gas
  - Multi-stage distillation: ~100 kWh/kg noble gas
  - Compression/storage: ~50 kWh/kg
  - Total: ~200 kWh/kg noble gas (very energy intensive)
Comparison to Earth sources:
  - Earth atmosphere: 0.93% Ar, 18 ppm Ne, 1 ppm Kr, 0.09 ppm Xe
  - 1000× to 1,000,000× higher than lunar regolith
  - Earth air separation vastly more economical
Trade-offs:
  - Import from Earth vs. extract from regolith
  - Early stages: Import essential (no alternative)
  - Long-term: Extraction only if absolutely critical
  - Most likely: Never economical to extract noble gases on Moon
Alternative: Import noble gases from Earth
  - Compressed gas cylinders: High pressure (150-200 bar)
  - Cryogenic liquid: Xe, Kr as liquids (saves mass/volume)
  - Reasonable mass penalty for Earth launch
  - Far cheaper than lunar extraction
Potential niche applications:
  - Emergency backup: Extract if Earth supply disrupted
  - Local use: Small quantities for welding, leak detection
  - Scientific experiments: Study solar wind implantation
Helium-3 co-extraction:
  - He-3 valuable for potential fusion (see helium3_cryogenic_separation_v0)
  - He separated first (lowest boiling point)
  - Noble gas extraction shares infrastructure with He-3 extraction
Separation efficiency:
  - Multi-stage distillation: 90-95% recovery
  - Cross-contamination: <1% between adjacent fractions
  - Requires 10-20 theoretical stages (trays or packing)
Cryogenic refrigeration:
  - Cascade refrigeration: Multiple refrigerants (NH3, CO2, CH4, etc.)
  - Or turbo-expander: Adiabatic expansion cooling
  - Extremely energy intensive (<10% Carnot efficiency typical)
Storage and handling:
  - High-pressure cylinders: 150-200 bar compressed gas
  - Cryogenic dewars: Liquid Xe (165K), Kr (120K)
  - Noble gases inert: No safety concerns (non-toxic, non-flammable)
  - Asphyxiation risk: Displace oxygen in confined spaces
Purity requirements:
  - Ion engines: 99.99% purity minimum (avoid cathode poisoning)
  - Welding: 99.9% adequate (small O2/N2 contamination acceptable)
  - Lighting: 99% adequate
Isotopic separation:
  - Natural isotope ratios: Ne (90% Ne-20, 10% Ne-22)
  - Ar (99.6% Ar-40, 0.3% Ar-36)
  - Kr, Xe: Multiple stable isotopes
  - Isotopic separation not typically needed (natural mix acceptable)
Research value:
  - Solar wind composition: Noble gas isotopes record solar wind history
  - Regolith exposure dating: Ne-21/Ne-22 ratio indicates exposure age
  - Scientific return: Study noble gas retention in regolith
Recommended approach:
  - Phase 1 (years 0-20): Import all noble gases from Earth
  - Phase 2 (years 20-50): Pilot noble gas extraction (research)
  - Phase 3 (years 50+): Consider noble gas extraction only if critical
  - Most likely: Import indefinitely (too expensive to extract locally)

raw.notes:
Aluminothermic (thermite-like) reduction of olivine to extract magnesium and silicon.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Primary reaction: 3Mg2SiO4 + 6Al → 2MgAl2O4 + 4MgO + 2AlSi + Si
Secondary reaction: 4MgO + 2AlSi → MgAl2O4 + 3Mg + 2Si (at 1000°C)
Temperature: 1000°C
Process: Exothermic thermite-style reduction
Olivine varieties: Forsterite (Mg2SiO4) preferred; fayalite (Fe2SiO4) similar
Reaction sequence:
  1. Initial aluminothermic reduction at 1000°C
  2. Continued reaction reduces remaining MgO
  3. Molten Mg tapped above 650°C melting point
  4. Products separate by density and melting point
Products:
  - MgAl2O4 (spinel): Refractory ceramic, further FFC reduction possible
  - Mg (magnesium metal): Liquid above 650°C, alloying element
  - Si (silicon): Semiconductor feedstock, alloying element
  - AlSi (aluminum-silicon alloy): Casting alloy, brazing filler
Product separation:
  - Mg taps as liquid (density 1.74 g/cm³, MP 650°C)
  - MgAl2O4 remains refractory solid (MP 2135°C)
  - Si and AlSi separate by density
Advantages: Relatively low temperature (1000°C)
Exothermic reaction reduces energy input
Multiple valuable products
Disadvantages: Requires aluminum metal input
Complex product mixture requires separation
Stoichiometry complex with two-stage reaction
Overall mass balance (approximate):
  - Mg output: ~51.4% of olivine mass
  - MgAl2O4: ~38.1%
  - Si metal: ~39.7%
  - AlSi alloy: ~13.7%
Applications: Alternative to FFC or Pidgeon for Mg extraction
Well-suited for lunar crater regions with olivine deposits

Magnesium collection: Condense vapor in cool chamber
Similar to vacuum pyrolysis but uses carbon reductant

Suitable for lunar south pole with continuous solar access
Alternative to Pidgeon or FFC routes

Generates hydrogen gas
