raw.notes:
Ostwald process for producing nitric acid from ammonia via catalytic oxidation.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Stage 1 - Ammonia oxidation: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O
Stage 2 - NO oxidation: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2
Stage 3 - Absorption: 3NO2 + H2O → 2HNO3 + NO (NO recycled)
Overall: NH3 + 2O2 → HNO3 + H2O
Temperature: 600-800°C for stage 1 (catalytic oxidation)
Pressure: 400-1000 kPa (4-10 bar)
Catalyst: Platinum on nickel (terrestrial) or tungsten carbide on nickel (lunar)
Process sequence:
  1. Ammonia vaporized and mixed with air/oxygen
  2. Catalytic oxidation to nitric oxide (NO) and water vapor
  3. Further oxidation of NO to nitrogen dioxide (NO2)
  4. Absorption of NO2 in water to form HNO3
  5. Unreacted NO recycled back to oxidation stage
Catalyst considerations:
  - Terrestrial: Platinum gauze (expensive, not available on Moon)
  - Lunar alternative: Tungsten carbide on nickel support
  - Nickel from Mond process (meteorite sources)
  - Tungsten from density-separated meteorite inclusions
Products:
  - HNO3 (nitric acid): Critical reagent for HCl production from NaCl
  - H2O (water): Process water, recyclable
Nitric acid applications:
  - React with NaCl to generate HCl gas: NaCl + HNO3 → HCl + NaNO3
  - Chemical synthesis, oxidizer, etching agent
  - Propellant oxidizer (when mixed with fuel)
Stoichiometry: NH3 (17g) + 2O2 (64g) → HNO3 (63g) + H2O (18g)
Mass fractions: 371% HNO3 from ammonia input
Nitrogen source: Haber-Bosch synthesis from volatile N2 extraction
Oxygen source: Water electrolysis or mineral reduction (abundant)
Advantages: Well-established industrial process
Enables HCl production from imported NaCl
HCl critical for artificial weathering and recycling loops
Disadvantages: Requires scarce nitrogen (from volatiles)
Pt catalyst unavailable (must use WC/Ni alternative)
Multi-stage process with gas handling
Lunar context: Nitrogen is severely scarce (~80 ppm in regolith volatiles)
Must be carefully husbanded and recycled
HNO3 → HCl → recycled as NaCl regeneration loop
Essential for unlocking chlorine chemistry with NaCl import

raw.notes:
Photon-Enhanced Thermionic Emission (PETE) power generation system.
Source: ellery-et-al-2022-metalysis-fray-farthing-chen-process
Purpose: Advanced power conversion combining photovoltaic and thermionic effects
Efficiency: Up to 50% (theoretical), 30-40% (practical)
Temperature: 1000-1500°C cathode temperature
Significantly more efficient than photovoltaics alone (~15-20%)
Process details:
  1. Concentrated solar radiation focused onto PETE cathode
  2. Photovoltaic stage: Photons excite electrons to conduction band
     - Semiconductor absorbs photons (hν > Eg)
     - Electron-hole pairs generated
     - Reduces effective work function
  3. Thermionic stage: Hot cathode emits electrons into vacuum
     - Temperature 1000-1500°C
     - Electrons overcome reduced work function barrier
     - Richardson-Dushman equation: J = AT² exp(-φ/kT)
  4. Electrons travel across vacuum gap to cold anode
  5. External circuit carries electrons back to cathode (generates power)
  6. Waste heat removed from anode via heat exchanger
  7. Can use waste heat for thermal processes (ISRU, FFC Cambridge)
PETE cathode structure:
  - Base: Tungsten or molybdenum substrate (high melting point)
  - Active layer: Aluminum-doped hematite (α-Fe2O3:Al)
    - Produced from ilmenite-derived iron + oxygen + Al dopant
    - Bandgap: ~2 eV (absorbs visible and near-IR)
    - Work function: ~1 eV (reduced by photon excitation)
  - Alternative: Cesiated surfaces (Ba-O-Cs coatings)
Physics:
  - Thermionic work function: φ = 1-2 eV typical
  - Photovoltaic reduces effective φ by photo-excitation
  - Combined effect: Higher current density than pure thermionic
  - Efficiency: η = (1 - Tc/Th) × (photon utilization factor)
Cathode temperature optimization:
  - Too low (<1000°C): Insufficient thermionic emission
  - Optimal (1200-1400°C): Maximum combined effect
  - Too high (>1500°C): Material degradation, thermal losses
Anode (collector):
  - Cool surface (<500°C) to maintain voltage
  - High work function material (not critical)
  - Heat extraction via radiator or heat pipe
Vacuum requirements:
  - High vacuum (10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁸ torr) to prevent electron scattering
  - Spacing: 1-10 μm gap (close spacing improves efficiency)
  - Challenges: Thermal expansion, alignment
Efficiency breakdown:
  - Photovoltaic stage: ~20-25% (photon → excited electrons)
  - Thermionic stage: ~25-30% (thermal → electron kinetic energy)
  - Combined: ~50% theoretical maximum
  - Practical: 30-40% (accounting for losses)
Comparison to other power systems:
  - Photovoltaics: ~15-20% (single junction), ~30% (multi-junction)
  - Thermionic: ~20% (pure thermionic, Russian nuclear reactors)
  - PETE: ~40-50% (combined photovoltaic + thermionic)
  - Lunar advantage: More efficient use of solar energy
Advantages: Very high efficiency (40-50%)
  Uses lunar materials (Fe2O3 from ilmenite, W from meteorites)
  Generates useful waste heat (1000+ °C) for ISRU
  No moving parts (solid-state)
  Long lifetime (no wear mechanisms)
Disadvantages: Requires high vacuum (challenging to maintain)
  High operating temperature (material constraints)
  Close cathode-anode spacing (precision alignment)
  Requires concentrated solar (not direct sunlight)
  Complex fabrication (thin-film cathode coatings)
Lunar context: Abundant solar energy (no atmosphere)
  14-day illumination periods (long operational time)
  High vacuum natural environment (Moon's surface)
  Can couple with ISRU thermal processes (use waste heat)
  Ideal for high-power applications (manufacturing, smelting)
Materials:
  - Cathode substrate: Tungsten (from meteorites, density separation)
  - Cathode coating: α-Fe2O3:Al (from ilmenite + aluminum)
  - Anode: Molybdenum, nickel, or stainless steel
  - Vacuum envelope: Fused silica or metal (lunar glass/metal)
Cathode coating synthesis:
  - Start with Fe from ilmenite reduction
  - Oxidize in O2 atmosphere: 2Fe + 3/2 O2 → Fe2O3 (hematite)
  - Dope with Al: Replace ~5% Fe with Al (improves conductivity)
  - Sinter at 1200-1400°C to densify
  - Result: α-Fe2O3:Al semiconductor with ~2 eV bandgap
Solar concentration:
  - Typical: 100-1000 suns (100,000-1,000,000 W/m²)
  - Fresnel lenses, parabolic mirrors, or heliostats
  - Achieves 1200-1400°C cathode temperature
Power output scaling:
  - Current density: 10-50 A/cm² (at 1200°C, 1.5V)
  - Power density: 15-75 W/cm²
  - For 1 kW output: 13-67 cm² cathode area
  - Modular design: Scale by number of converters
Waste heat utilization:
  - Anode at 500-800°C (substantial thermal energy)
  - Use for FFC Cambridge (900-1100°C after heat pump)
  - Or other thermal processes (glass melting, sintering)
  - Combined heat and power (CHP): Overall >70% energy utilization
Vacuum maintenance:
  - Getter materials: Absorb residual gases (Ba, Ti getters)
  - Seal integrity: High-temperature seals (glass-metal, ceramic)
  - Lunar vacuum: Natural environment (10⁻¹⁴ torr)
  - Can operate in lunar ambient vacuum (no envelope needed!)
Operational modes:
  - Day: PETE power generation (14 Earth days continuous)
  - Night: Shutdown, cool down (14 Earth days)
  - Thermal cycling: Design for repeated cycling
Reliability and lifetime:
  - Solid-state (no moving parts): Long lifetime expected
  - Material degradation: Cathode coating evaporation at high T
  - Estimated lifetime: 10-20 years (with proper design)
Development status (terrestrial):
  - Research stage (laboratory demonstrations)
  - Stanford, MIT research programs
  - Not yet commercial
  - Significant engineering challenges remain
Lunar advantages over terrestrial:
  - Natural vacuum (no envelope needed or simplified)
  - Concentrated solar easily achievable
  - Heat rejection via radiation (no atmosphere)
  - Long illumination periods (14-day "day")
Integration with lunar ISRU:
  1. Solar concentration → PETE cathode → electrical power
  2. PETE waste heat → FFC Cambridge electrolysis → metals + O2
  3. Metals → manufacturing (structures, machines)
  4. Electrical power → water electrolysis, mining, robotics
  5. Closed-loop energy conversion system
Efficiency comparison (solar → useful work):
  - PV + resistive heating: 15% electric, 85% waste (unusable)
  - PETE + waste heat recovery: 40% electric, 50% useful heat, 10% loss
  - Net useful energy: PETE vastly superior for thermal processes
Research needs:
  - Optimize cathode coating (composition, thickness, doping)
  - Improve vacuum sealing (or open-vacuum lunar design)
  - Thermal management (heat pipes, radiators)
  - Cathode-anode spacing control (thermal expansion compensation)
  - Long-term stability testing (evaporation, degradation)
Recommended development timeline:
  - Phase 1 (years 0-10): Import terrestrial solar panels (PV)
  - Phase 2 (years 10-30): Develop PETE prototypes on Moon
  - Phase 3 (years 30+): Deploy PETE for high-power ISRU applications
Critical enabler for:
  - Large-scale FFC Cambridge (requires electrical + thermal energy)
  - Smelting operations (coupled power + heat)
  - Materials processing (manufacturing infrastructure)
Comparison to nuclear power:
  - Nuclear: Continuous power (day and night)
  - PETE: Intermittent (14-day on, 14-day off)
  - Nuclear: Higher complexity, safety concerns, waste
  - PETE: Simpler, safer, but requires energy storage for night
Energy storage pairing:
  - PETE day: Generate power + charge batteries
  - Night: Discharge batteries or shutdown non-critical loads
  - Alternatively: Locate near polar craters (near-continuous sunlight)
Polar deployment:
  - Peaks of eternal light: 80-90% sunlight availability
  - Shackleton crater rim: Nearly continuous illumination
  - Ideal for PETE (minimizes cycling, maximizes uptime)

energy_model.notes: High temperature carbothermal reduction at 850°C (1 kg batch)

raw.notes:
KREEP basalt modeled as basalt_aggregate until a dedicated KREEP feedstock exists.
Extraction of elemental phosphorus from apatite (calcium phosphate) in KREEP regions.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt
Reaction: 4H3PO4 + 16C → P4 + 6H2 + 16CO (simplified from Ca3(PO4)2)
Or: Ca3(PO4)2 + 5C → 3CaO + 2P + 5CO (then P4 formation)
Temperature: 850°C (phosphorus vaporizes)
Process: Carbothermal reduction in sealed retort
Purpose: Extract phosphorus from KREEP minerals
Essential element for life support (agriculture)
Electronic materials (phosphorus doping)
Process details:
  1. Apatite [Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH)] from KREEP basalts
  2. Mix with carbon (reducing agent)
  3. Heat to 850°C in sealed retort (excludes oxygen)
  4. Phosphorus vaporizes as P4 molecules
  5. Condense phosphorus vapor underwater (safety)
  6. Store as white phosphorus under water
  7. CaO (quicklime) remains as solid residue
Products:
  - P4 (white phosphorus): Highly reactive, toxic, pyrophoric
  - H2 (hydrogen): By-product gas
  - CO (carbon monoxide): Recyclable
  - CaO (calcium oxide): Useful for various processes
KREEP regions:
  - Oceanus Procellarum and Imbrium Basin (northwest nearside)
  - Enriched in K (potassium), REE (rare earth elements), P (phosphorus)
  - P concentration: ~2× terrestrial soil (still depleted overall)
  - Apatite: Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH) - primary P mineral
  - Concentrated enough for economic extraction
White phosphorus handling:
  - Extremely pyrophoric (ignites in air at 34°C)
  - Toxic (lethal dose ~50 mg)
  - Stored underwater to prevent air contact
  - Converted to red phosphorus (safer allotrope) by heating to 250°C
Phosphorus applications:
  - Agriculture: Phosphate fertilizers (critical for food production)
  - Life support: Plant growth in habitats
  - Electronics: Phosphorus doping (n-type semiconductor)
  - Chemical synthesis: Phosphoric acid, phosphates
  - Incendiaries/pyrotechnics (white P)
Stoichiometry: Ca3(PO4)2 (310g) + 5C (60g) → 3CaO (168g) + 2P (62g) + 5CO (140g)
Mass fractions: 24.7% P, 89.0% CaO, 141% CO from apatite
Red phosphorus production: Heat white P to 250°C in sealed vessel
  - Much safer (not pyrophoric)
  - Less reactive
  - Preferred form for most applications
Advantages: Only viable source of phosphorus on Moon
KREEP localized and accessible
CaO by-product useful
CO recyclable
Disadvantages: High toxicity and reactivity of white P
KREEP only in specific regions (not globally distributed)
High temperature requirement
Safety hazards in handling
Lunar context: Phosphorus absolutely essential for agriculture
Long-term settlement requires food production
No alternative source on Moon
Must extract from KREEP despite challenges
Careful handling protocols essential
Red phosphorus conversion recommended immediately

raw.notes:
Pidgeon process for direct magnesium metal extraction from olivine using quicklime.
Source: Lunar-Demandite.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: Mg2SiO4 + 2CaO → Ca2SiO4 + 2Mg (vapor)
Temperature: >1000°C (typically 1100-1200°C)
Pressure: Vacuum or low pressure (drives Mg vaporization)
Process: Thermal reduction with CaO in sealed retort
Magnesium boiling point: 1091°C (vaporizes during process)
Product collection: Mg vapor condensed on cool surfaces
Products:
  - Mg metal (vapor→solid): Lightweight structural metal, alloying element
  - Ca2SiO4 (calcium silicate): Cement component, slag
Calcium oxide source: Anorthite carbothermal reduction or limestone calcination
Process details:
  1. Mix powdered olivine with CaO in stoichiometric ratio
  2. Heat mixture in sealed retort under vacuum
  3. Mg vaporizes and migrates to condenser
  4. Condense Mg on cool surface as solid metal
  5. Ca2SiO4 remains as solid residue
Advantages: Direct metal production (not oxide)
No electrolysis required
Simple chemistry with abundant lunar materials
Proven terrestrial process (dominant Mg production method)
Disadvantages: High temperature requirement
Requires vacuum/low pressure system
Vapor handling complexity
CaO input requirement
Stoichiometry: Mg2SiO4 (140.7g) + 2CaO (112.2g) → 2Mg (48.6g) + Ca2SiO4 (172.2g)
Mg yield from olivine: 34.5% by mass
Ca2SiO4 yield: 98.5% from combined inputs (123% from olivine alone)
Most economic terrestrial process for Mg production
Well-suited for lunar ISRU with CaO from anorthite
Alternative to FFC Cambridge or aluminothermic routes
Vacuum environment on Moon advantageous for Mg vapor collection

raw.notes:
Extraction of water ice from permanently shadowed craters at lunar poles.
Source: Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Location: Permanently shadowed craters (PSCs) at north and south poles
Temperature: ~40 K (-233°C) in PSCs
Concentration: 5.6% ± 2.9% by mass (LCROSS impact data)
Purpose: Extract water for life support, propellant, hydrogen source
Higher concentration than volatile extraction from regolith
Process details:
  1. Heliostats on peaks of eternal light reflect sunlight to PSCs
  2. Solar arrays in PSC powered by reflected light
  3. Drill into frozen regolith to depth (subsurface ice)
  4. Option A - Direct heating: Heat ice directly, capture sublimed vapor
  5. Option B - Heater insertion: Insert heaters into boreholes
  6. Ice sublimes/melts, vapor captured in cold trap canopy
  7. Condense water vapor to liquid or keep as ice
Products:
  - H2O (water ice/liquid): 5.6% average, up to 8.5% in some locations
  - Dry regolith: Processed material
Ice characteristics:
  - Rock-hard when frozen (~40 K)
  - Drilling difficult (similar to drilling concrete)
  - May be in layers or pockets (not uniformly distributed)
  - Subsurface ice insulated by dry regolith overburden
Water ice deposits:
  - Total PSC area: >31,000 km² (both poles)
  - Estimated inventory: 3-6 × 10¹² kg (3-6 billion tonnes)
  - Cabeus crater (south pole): High concentration region
  - 40+ craters at north pole with water potential
Energy challenges:
  - PSCs permanently shadowed (no direct sunlight)
  - Heliostats required: Reflect sunlight from peaks of eternal light
  - Distance: ~20 km vertical and horizontal
  - Three heliostats minimum for continuous coverage
Heliostat system:
  - Mirrors on peaks of eternal light (continuous solar access)
  - Beam sunlight to PSC floor (photovoltaics or direct heating)
  - Complex pointing and tracking
  - Alternative: Nuclear power for PSC operations
Stoichiometry: 1000 kg frozen regolith → 56 kg water ice (5.6%)
Comparison to volatile extraction:
  - Polar ice: 5.6% H2O by mass
  - Regolith volatiles: 0.046% H by mass (~0.041% H2O equivalent)
  - Polar ice ~140x higher water concentration
Advantages: Much higher concentration than regolith volatiles
Large total inventory (billions of tonnes)
Direct water extraction (not just H)
Disadvantages: Extreme environment (40 K, permanently dark)
Complex infrastructure (heliostats, drilling, heating)
Rugged terrain (SPA basin: 11 km elevation changes)
Distance from potential base sites (peaks of eternal light)
Lunar context: Critical water source for life support
Hydrogen for reduction processes (ilmenite, etc.)
Oxygen via electrolysis
Propellant/oxidizer (though wasteful of scarce resource)
Sustainability concern: Burning H2/O2 as propellant unsustainable
Better uses: Life support recycling, chemical processes
Alternative propulsion: Solar-electric, electromagnetic launchers

entities.name: Rare earth element extraction from KREEP basalts

raw.name: Rare earth element extraction from KREEP basalts

energy_model.notes: Energy-intensive acid leaching, separation, and calcination

time_model.notes: Multi-stage leaching, extraction, and purification

raw.notes:
KREEP basalt modeled as basalt_aggregate until a dedicated KREEP feedstock exists.
REE oxide concentrate modeled as reduced_metal_oxides for now.
Rare earth element (REE) extraction from KREEP basalts (advanced process).
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Purpose: Extract REE for permanent magnets (NdFeB), superconductors (NbTi), catalysts
KREEP: Potassium (K), Rare Earth Elements (REE), Phosphorus (P) enriched basalts
Concentration: ~1200 ppm average REE (0.12%), up to 5× higher than Earth
WARNING: Complex, energy-intensive process - not suitable for first-generation ISRU
Process details:
  1. Locate KREEP regions using gamma-ray spectroscopy
     - Detect U, Th signatures (correlate with REE)
     - U/Th ratio ~0.27 typical for KREEP
     - Imbrium basin, Oceanus Procellarum highest concentrations
  2. Mine and crush KREEP basalt ore
  3. Roast ore at 600°C to oxidize Ce³⁺ to Ce⁴⁺ (if Ce separation desired)
  4. Acid leaching with concentrated H2SO4 (or HCl)
     - Heat to 80-100°C for several hours
     - REE dissolve as sulfates or chlorides
     - REE³⁺ + 3/2 H2SO4 → REE2(SO4)3 + 3/2 H2
  5. Filter leach liquor from insoluble residue
  6. Solvent extraction for REE concentration and separation
     - Organic extractants: D2EHPA, Cyanex, TODGA
     - Multiple stages for individual REE separation
     - pH-dependent extraction selectivity
  7. Strip REE from organic phase with acid
  8. Precipitate REE as oxalates: REE³⁺ + oxalic acid → REE2(C2O4)3
  9. Calcinate oxalates to oxides: REE2(C2O4)3 → REE2O3 + CO + CO2
  10. Further purification if individual REE needed (beyond scope)
Products:
  - Mixed rare earth oxides (REO): ~0.12% of ore mass, mixture of La, Ce, Nd, Y, etc.
  - Leach residue: Depleted ore, may contain valuable minerals
  - Acids: Partially recycled
REE concentration in KREEP:
  - Total REE: ~1200 ppm (0.12%) average
  - Y: ~300 ppm (most abundant)
  - Ce: ~300 ppm
  - Nd: ~180 ppm (critical for magnets)
  - La: ~150 ppm
  - Sm: ~50 ppm
  - Gd: ~50 ppm
  - Pr: ~40 ppm
  - Dy: ~30 ppm (critical for magnets)
  - Others: Eu (~3-5 ppm), Tb, Ho, Er, Yb, Lu (each <30 ppm)
KREEP detection:
  - Gamma-ray spectroscopy: Detect U (3-10 ppm), Th (10-40 ppm)
  - U/Th ratio ~0.27 diagnostic for KREEP
  - Lunar Prospector gamma-ray data shows hotspots
  - Procellarum KREEP Terrane (PKT) richest region
REE applications (critical for advanced technology):
  - NdFeB magnets: Strongest permanent magnets (Nd, Dy additions)
  - Electric motors: High-power-density motors (robotics, spacecraft)
  - Generators: Lightweight, high-efficiency power generation
  - Superconductors: NbTi superconducting wire (Nb is REE-associated)
  - Catalysts: La, Ce for various chemical processes
  - Lasers: Nd:YAG lasers (Nd-doped yttrium aluminum garnet)
  - Phosphors: Eu, Tb for displays and lighting
  - Batteries: La in NiMH batteries
Stoichiometry (example, Ce):
  - Ce2O3 + 3H2SO4 → Ce2(SO4)3 + 3H2O (leaching)
  - Ce2(SO4)3 + 3 H2C2O4 → Ce2(C2O4)3 + 3H2SO4 (precipitation)
  - Ce2(C2O4)3 → Ce2O3 + 3CO + 3CO2 (calcination at 800°C)
Separation challenges:
  - REE have very similar chemistry (all 3+ cations)
  - Separation requires many stages (10-50 extraction stages)
  - Extremely complex process (solvent extraction cascades)
  - Individual REE separation beyond first-gen ISRU capability
Mixed REO vs. separated REE:
  - Mixed REO: Easier, 10-20 extraction stages
  - Separated REE: Extremely difficult, requires specialized equipment
  - For first lunar use: Mixed REO may be acceptable
  - Refine to pure REE only if absolutely necessary
Advantages: KREEP concentration 5× higher than typical Earth ores
  Multiple valuable elements (REE, U, Th, P, K)
  Enables high-tech applications (magnets, superconductors)
Disadvantages: Extremely complex process (many stages)
  Energy intensive (acid production, leaching, calcination)
  Requires exotic reagents (organic extractants)
  Low concentration (0.12% even in KREEP)
  Not economical for first-generation ISRU
Lunar context: KREEP regions well-mapped (Procellarum, Imbrium)
  Essential for advanced manufacturing (motors, generators, sensors)
  Likely deferred to later ISRU stages (after basics established)
  But critical for long-term sustainability
Alternative processing:
  - Pyrometallurgical: High-temp chlorination/fluorination
  - Ion exchange: Similar to solvent extraction but solid resin
  - Electrochemical: Direct electrolysis of REE salts
Uranium and Thorium co-extraction:
  - U and Th also leach with REE (both 4+, 3+ cations)
  - Must separate or manage radioactive elements
  - U/Th potentially valuable for nuclear power
  - Or hazard requiring careful disposal
Phosphorus co-extraction:
  - KREEP rich in phosphate minerals (apatite)
  - P extracted as phosphoric acid (H3PO4)
  - Valuable for fertilizer (agriculture on Moon/Mars)
  - Or phosphorus for semiconductors (dopant)
Potassium recovery:
  - K dissolves as sulfate or chloride
  - Separate from REE by solvent extraction
  - Valuable for fertilizer, glass production
Environmental/safety concerns:
  - Concentrated acids (H2SO4, HCl) hazardous
  - Radioactive U, Th require shielding and containment
  - Organic solvents (flammable, toxic)
  - Must be closed-loop, zero-release system
Scale requirements:
  - 1 tonne KREEP ore → ~1.2 kg mixed REO
  - For 1 kg pure Nd: ~6 tonnes KREEP ore (if 180 ppm Nd)
  - Large-scale mining required for useful quantities
Energy analysis:
  - Acid production: ~10 kWh/kg acid (if from scratch)
  - Leaching/heating: ~20 kWh/tonne ore
  - Solvent extraction: ~50 kWh/kg REO
  - Calcination: ~5 kWh/kg REO
  - Total: ~150 kWh/kg REO (very energy intensive)
Comparison to Earth REE processing:
  - Earth: ~0.02-0.1% REE typical (bastnäsite, monazite)
  - KREEP: ~0.12% REE (slightly better)
  - Similar complexity, similar energy costs
Trade-offs:
  - Import REE from Earth vs. extract from KREEP
  - Early stages: Import likely cheaper
  - Long-term: In-situ extraction necessary for self-sufficiency
  - Critical decision point: When does KREEP mining become viable?
Recommended timeline:
  - Phase 1 (years 0-10): Import REE from Earth
  - Phase 2 (years 10-30): Develop KREEP processing pilot plant
  - Phase 3 (years 30+): Full-scale KREEP mining and REE extraction

raw.notes:
Mining of ice-bearing regolith from permanently shadowed craters.

Location: North and south pole PSCs
Temperature: ~40 K (-233°C)
Ice concentration: 5.6% ± 2.9% by mass

Operational considerations:
- PSCs are permanently dark (no direct sunlight)
- Heliostats required: Reflect sunlight from peaks of eternal light
- Heliostat distance: ~20 km vertical and horizontal
- Alternative: Nuclear power for PSC operations

Mining challenges:
- Ice-cemented regolith is rock-hard (similar to concrete)
- Requires drilling equipment (not just scooping)
- Lower excavation rate than loose mare/highlands regolith
- Higher energy per kg due to drilling
- Extreme cold requires specialized equipment

Rate justification:
- Mare regolith (loose): 100 kg/hr with labor bot
- PSC regolith (ice-cement): 50 kg/hr with labor bot + drilling equipment
- Factor of 2x reduction due to hardness

Energy justification:
- Mare regolith: 0.05 kWh/kg (simple scooping)
- PSC regolith: 0.5 kWh/kg (drilling + heliostat operation)
- Factor of 10x increase for drilling hard material

Infrastructure requirements:
- Heliostat array on peaks of eternal light
- Communication relay (PSCs are in radio shadow)
- Thermal management (equipment must operate at 40 K or be insulated)
- Power transmission from heliostats or nuclear source

Source: Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
LCROSS impact data (Cabeus crater, 2009)

raw.notes:
Thermal extraction and fractional distillation of solar-wind volatiles from lunar regolith.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, I-SAIRAS-2020
Process: Heat regolith to evolve implanted volatiles, then fractionally distill
Temperature: 700-1200°C (higher for complete volatile release)
Purpose: Extract H, He, C, N volatiles from regolith
Critical source of scarce light elements
Process details:
  1. Excavate regolith from upper 2-3m (gardened by impacts)
  2. Heat in furnace to 700°C (most volatiles) or 1200°C (complete)
  3. Evolved gases collected: H2, He, CO, CO2, CH4, N2, H2O
  4. Fractional distillation by condensation temperature:
     - He: 4.2 K (condenses first at lowest temp)
     - H2: 20 K
     - N2: 77 K
     - CO: 81 K
     - CH4: 109 K
     - CO2: 194 K
     - H2O: 373 K (condenses last)
Products (average concentrations from highlands regolith):
  - H: 46 ppm (mostly as H2, some in H2O, CH4)
  - 4He: 14 ppm (noble gas)
  - C: 124 ppm (CO, CO2, CH4 mixture - most abundant volatile!)
  - N: 81 ppm (mostly N2)
  - Also: F, Cl, S in trace amounts
Solar-wind implantation:
  - Volatiles implanted in mineral grains over millions of years
  - Concentration approximately constant to 2-3m depth (gardening)
  - Ilmenite-rich regolith has highest volatile retention
  - Mature regolith (long surface exposure) richest
Volatile yields (typical):
  - H2O equivalent: ~900 J/kg/°C heating energy
  - Total volatiles: <300 ppm by mass (0.03%)
  - Carbon most abundant volatile (after H)
Stoichiometry: 1000 kg regolith → ~0.26 kg total volatiles
Critical elements:
  - H: Water, hydrogen reduction, life support
  - He: Inert atmosphere, leak detection, (3He fusion fuel)
  - C: Plastics, reducing agent, FFC anodes, life support
  - N: Fertilizer, Haber-Bosch, life support, propellant oxidizer
Advantages: Only source of light volatiles (H, He, C, N) on Moon
Simple thermal process
Regolith abundant everywhere
No chemical reagents needed
Disadvantages: Very low concentrations (<300 ppm)
Large mass throughput required
Energy intensive for low yield
Cryogenic separation complexity
Lunar context: Absolutely critical for long-term sustainability
No other source of C, N, He on Moon
Hydrogen supplemented by polar water ice
Must carefully husband these scarce resources
Ilmenite beneficiation increases volatile concentration
3He valuable for future fusion (4-30 ppb, extract with other volatiles)

raw.name: Reverse water-gas shift reaction

energy_model.notes: Endothermic reaction at 400-600°C

time_model.notes: Catalytic reduction time

raw.notes:
Reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) reaction for converting CO2 to CO using hydrogen.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Mars ISRU literature
Reaction: CO2 + H2 → CO + H2O (endothermic)
Temperature: 400-600°C
Catalyst: Iron or nickel based catalysts
Process: Catalytic reduction of CO2 to CO
Purpose: Generate CO for Mond/carbonyl processes
Alternative to Boudouard reaction (no carbon consumption)
Produce syngas (CO + H2 mixture) for chemical synthesis
Thermodynamics:
  - Endothermic (ΔH = +41 kJ/mol, requires heat input)
  - Equilibrium limited (not 100% conversion)
  - Favored at higher temperatures
Products:
  - CO (carbon monoxide): Mond process feedstock, syngas component
  - H2O (water): Electrolyzed to recycle H2 + produce O2
Water electrolysis: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
  - Recycles hydrogen
  - Net: CO2 + energy → CO + ½O2
Stoichiometry: CO2 (44g) + H2 (2g) → CO (28g) + H2O (18g)
Mass fractions: 63.6% CO, 40.9% H2O from inputs
Comparison to alternatives:
  - Boudouard: C + CO2 → 2CO (uses carbon, higher temp)
  - Bosch: CO2 + 2H2 → C + 2H2O (produces solid carbon)
  - Sabatier: CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O (produces methane)
RWGS advantages: Uses less H2 than Sabatier
Produces CO directly (no carbon intermediate)
Lower temperature than Boudouard
Disadvantages: Endothermic (requires energy input)
Equilibrium limited conversion
Lower selectivity than Sabatier or Bosch
Applications:
  - CO production for Mond/carbonyl metal purification
  - Syngas generation (CO + H2 for Fischer-Tropsch, methanol synthesis)
  - Alternative to Boudouard when carbon is scarce
  - Mars ISRU (CO2 abundant in atmosphere)
Lunar context: Useful when CO needed but carbon is scarce
Hydrogen from water electrolysis or volatiles
Catalyst: Iron from ilmenite or nickel from meteorites
Can be coupled with water electrolysis for H2 recycling
Alternative pathway in carbon management network

Used on ISS for CO2 recycling

Coupled with carbothermal processes for complete mineral processing

raw.notes:
Siemens process stage 2: Chemical vapor deposition of ultra-pure polysilicon.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt
Reaction: SiHCl3 + H2 → Si + 3HCl (at 1150°C)
Temperature: 1150°C (resistive heating of silicon seed rods)
Process: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) on heated silicon rods
Purpose: Deposit ultra-pure polysilicon for electronics and solar cells
Second stage of Siemens process
Process details:
  1. SiHCl3 vapor (from stage 1) mixed with excess H2
  2. Flow over resistively-heated silicon seed rods at 1150°C
  3. SiHCl3 thermally decomposes, depositing Si on rods
  4. HCl gas released, condensed, and recycled to stage 1
  5. Rods grow in diameter over 24-48 hours
  6. Break rods into chunks (polysilicon)
Products:
  - Polysilicon (ultra-pure, 9-11 nines purity)
  - HCl gas (recycled to stage 1 chlorination)
Silicon seed rods:
  - Initial thin rods of metallurgical or polysilicon
  - Electrically heated by passing current through them
  - Si deposits on surface, growing rod diameter
  - Can grow from ~8mm to 150-200mm diameter
Stoichiometry: SiHCl3 (135.5g) + H2 (2g) → Si (28g) + 3HCl (109.5g)
Mass fractions: 20.7% Si, 80.7% HCl from SiHCl3 input
HCl recycling: All HCl returned to stage 1
Net process: Metallurgical Si → Ultra-pure polysilicon (via closed loop)
Purity achieved: 99.9999999% to 99.999999999% (9N to 11N)
Impurity levels: <1 ppb (part per billion) for most elements
Advantages: Highest purity silicon available
Complete HCl recycling (closed loop with stage 1)
Standard industrial process (well-proven)
Suitable for both electronics and solar applications
Disadvantages: Extremely energy intensive (150-200 kWh/kg total)
Very slow (1-2 days per batch)
High temperature requirement
Batch process (not continuous)
Applications:
  - Electronics: Czochralski → single crystal → wafers → ICs
  - Solar cells: High-efficiency (20-25%) photovoltaics
  - Sensors: Photodetectors, pressure sensors, MEMS
Lunar/space context: Critical for in-situ electronics manufacturing
Solar cells for power generation
Sensors and computing for automation
Alternative: Float-zone refining for even higher purity (12N)
Next step: Czochralski or float-zone for single-crystal silicon

raw.notes:
Siemens process stage 1: Silicon chlorination to produce trichlorosilane.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt
Reaction: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2 (at 300°C)
Temperature: 300°C
Process: Gas-solid chlorination in fluidized bed
Purpose: Purify metallurgical-grade silicon to semiconductor/solar grade
First stage of two-stage Siemens process
Process details:
  1. Metallurgical Si powder (99% pure from carbothermal/FFC)
  2. React with HCl gas at 300°C in fluidized bed
  3. SiHCl3 (trichlorosilane) forms as liquid (BP 31.8°C)
  4. Distillation purifies SiHCl3 (removes impurities)
  5. H2 gas by-product collected
Products:
  - SiHCl3 (trichlorosilane): Intermediate for polysilicon production
  - H2 (hydrogen): Recycled for stage 2 reduction
Metallurgical silicon sources:
  - Carbothermal reduction: CaAl2Si2O8 + 4C → 2Si + ...
  - FFC Cambridge: SiO2 → Si + O2
  - Carbothermal methane: MgSiO3 + 2CH4 → Si + ...
SiHCl3 purification:
  - Fractional distillation removes metal chlorides (BCl3, PCl3, etc.)
  - Achieves ppb-level purity (parts per billion)
  - Critical for electronics and high-efficiency solar cells
Stoichiometry: Si (28g) + 3HCl (109.5g) → SiHCl3 (135.5g) + H2 (2g)
Mass fractions: 483% SiHCl3, 7.2% H2 from Si input
HCl recycling: Stage 2 regenerates HCl for re-use here
Overall Siemens process (both stages):
  - This stage: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2
  - Stage 2: SiHCl3 + H2 → Si + 3HCl (see companion process)
  - Net: Metallurgical Si → Ultra-pure polysilicon
Advantages: Achieves ultra-high purity (9-11 nines: 99.9999999-99.999999999%)
HCl fully recycled between two stages
Standard industrial process for semiconductor Si
Disadvantages: Two-stage process complexity
Energy intensive overall
Requires HCl (from NaCl-based chlorine chemistry)
Lunar/space applications: Essential for electronics manufacturing
High-efficiency solar cells (>20% vs <15% for metallurgical)
Integrated circuits, sensors, processors
See also: Czochralski process (single-crystal growth from polysilicon)

energy_model.notes: H2-O2 flame temperature ~2800°C for SiCl4 oxidation

time_model.notes: Vapor phase deposition onto substrate

raw.notes:
High-purity fused silica glass production via flame hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride.
Source: FFC-process-for-deep-ISRU.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: SiCl4 + 2H2 + O2 → SiO2 + 4HCl
Temperature: H2-O2 flame (~2800°C)
Purpose: Optical-grade fused silica for optics, fiber optics, and precision applications
Process details:
  1. Silicon tetrachloride vapor (from carbochlorination or Siemens)
  2. Hydrogen and oxygen gases (from water electrolysis)
  3. SiCl4 vapor enters H2-O2 flame in deposition chamber
  4. Flame hydrolysis: SiCl4 oxidizes to SiO2 particles
  5. SiO2 particles deposit on rotating substrate (mandrel)
  6. Build up glassy soot layer
  7. Sinter soot to dense fused silica (1600°C consolidation)
  8. HCl vapor captured and recycled
  9. Cool and remove fused silica blank
Products:
  - Fused silica glass: Optical-grade, ultra-pure
  - HCl gas: Captured and recycled to SiCl4 production
Stoichiometry: SiCl4 (169.9g) + 2H2 (4g) + O2 (32g) → SiO2 (60.1g) + 4HCl (145.8g)
Mass yields: 35.4% SiO2, 85.8% HCl (recycled)
Purity: >99.999% SiO2 (5 nines)
  - Lower OH content than natural quartz
  - Extremely low metal impurities
Optical properties:
  - Transmittance: >90% in UV to near-IR (200-2500 nm)
  - Low fluorescence
  - Excellent homogeneity
  - Controlled refractive index
Applications:
  - Optical lenses and mirrors: High transmittance, low scatter
  - Fiber optic preforms: Communication fibers
  - UV optics: Transmits down to 180 nm
  - Precision windows: High purity, no bubbles
  - Semiconductor lithography: UV steppers
  - Crucibles: For Czochralski silicon growth
Advantages: Extremely high purity (chemical vapor deposition)
  No contamination from melting crucible_refractory
  Controlled composition and properties
  Complete HCl recycling (85.8% by mass)
  Scalable to large blanks
Disadvantages: Energy intensive (flame temperature)
  Requires pure SiCl4 feedstock
  Multi-step process (deposition + sintering)
  Slow deposition rate
Process variations:
  - Outside vapor deposition (OVD): Soot on rotating mandrel
  - Inside vapor deposition (IVD): Soot inside tube
  - Vapor axial deposition (VAD): Axial growth
Flame chemistry:
  - 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O + heat (exothermic combustion)
  - SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl (hydrolysis)
  - Net: SiCl4 + 2H2 + O2 → SiO2 + 4HCl
Sintering step (consolidation):
  - Porous soot heated to 1600°C in inert atmosphere
  - Densifies to transparent fused silica (2.2 g/cm³)
  - Critical for optical quality
Lunar context: Essential for photovoltaics and optics
  Enables communication (fiber optics)
  Precision manufacturing (lithography)
  Scientific instruments (telescopes, spectrometers)
Comparison to natural quartz:
  - Natural: Crystalline, anisotropic, contains impurities
  - Fused silica: Amorphous, isotropic, ultra-pure
  - Fused silica superior for most optical applications
HCl recycling critical:
  - 85.8% of input mass is HCl product
  - HCl + Si → SiHCl3 (Siemens process)
  - Or HCl + SiO2 + C → SiCl4 (carbochlorination)
  - Closed-loop chlorine chemistry
Alternate route to fused silica:
  - Direct melting of quartz sand (1710°C)
  - Lower purity, higher contamination
  - Flame hydrolysis preferred for optical grade
Trade-offs:
  - Complexity vs. purity: Flame hydrolysis more complex but higher purity
  - Energy: Both require high temperatures (1600-2800°C)
  - Feedstock: SiCl4 route requires chlorine chemistry infrastructure

raw.notes:
Solvay process for producing sodium carbonate (soda ash) from salt and limestone.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Stage 1 - Ammoniation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl
Stage 2 - Calcination: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 (heating to 175°C)
Stage 3 - Ammonia recovery: 2NH4Cl + CaO → 2NH3 + CaCl2 + H2O
Overall reaction: 2NaCl + CaCO3 ⇌ Na2CO3 + CaCl2
Temperature: Room temp for stage 1, 175°C for stage 2, elevated for stage 3
Process: Multi-stage industrial process for alkali production
Process flow:
  1. Dissolve NaCl in water (brine)
  2. Bubble NH3 and CO2 through brine
  3. NaHCO3 (sodium bicarbonate) precipitates, filter
  4. Heat NaHCO3 to produce Na2CO3 and recycle CO2
  5. Recover NH3 from NH4Cl using quicklime (CaO)
  6. Recycle NH3 and CO2 to step 2
Products:
  - Na2CO3 (sodium carbonate/soda ash): Glass, quartz growth, Se extraction
  - CaCl2 (calcium chloride): FFC Cambridge electrolyte replenishment
Sodium carbonate applications (critical):
  - Quartz crystal synthesis: Na2CO3 + SiO2 ↔ Na2SiO3 + CO2
  - Selenium extraction: FeSe + Na2CO3 + O2 → Se + FeO + CO2
  - Glass production: Flux for silica melting
  - Chemical synthesis: Alkali source
Reagent recycling:
  - NH3: 97-98% recycled (minimal losses)
  - CO2: 100% recycled in loop
  - CaO from anorthite: CaAl2Si2O8 + 4C → CaO + ...
  - Net consumption: Only NaCl and CaCO3 (or CaO)
Stoichiometry: 2NaCl (117g) + CaCO3 (100g) → Na2CO3 (106g) + CaCl2 (111g)
Mass fractions: 90.7% Na2CO3, 94.9% CaCl2 from NaCl input
Advantages: Proven industrial process (150+ years)
Complete reagent recycling (NH3, CO2)
Produces valuable CaCl2 for FFC
Simple chemistry with available lunar materials
Disadvantages: Multi-stage complexity
Requires NaCl import (scarce on Moon)
Calcium carbonate from CaO + CO2 (preprocessing)
Lunar context: NaCl is precious imported reagent
Solvay enables one NaCl import to produce Na2CO3
CaCl2 by-product replenishes FFC electrolyte
Closes multiple chemical loops
Critical for quartz sensors and selenium photosensors
Alternative: Direct reaction 2NaCl + CaCO3 at high temp (less efficient)

raw.notes:
Contact process for producing sulfuric acid from sulfur dioxide.
Source: Lunar-Demandite.txt, Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Stage 1 - Oxidation: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 (reversible, exothermic)
Stage 2 - Absorption: SO3 + H2O → H2SO4 (highly exothermic)
Catalyst: Vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) at 450°C
Process: Catalytic oxidation followed by absorption
Purpose: Produce sulfuric acid for chemical processing
Ilmenite acid leaching: FeTiO3 + 2H2SO4 → products
Selenium extraction: Na2SeO3 + H2SO4 → Se + ...
Process details:
  1. SO2 gas (from troilite roasting or sulfur combustion)
  2. Mix with oxygen (from mineral reduction processes)
  3. Pass over V2O5 catalyst at 450°C
  4. SO3 produced (equilibrium reaction, ~98% conversion)
  5. Absorb SO3 in water or oleum
  6. Concentrated H2SO4 produced
Products:
  - H2SO4 (sulfuric acid): 96-98% concentrated acid
SO2 sources:
  - Troilite roasting: 4FeS + 7O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 4SO2
  - Sulfur combustion: S + O2 → SO2
Catalyst: V2O5 (vanadium pentoxide)
  - Not abundant on Moon (V rare)
  - Small amounts needed (catalyst not consumed)
  - May need Earth import initially
  - Alternative: Platinum (also rare), iron oxide (less efficient)
Sulfuric acid applications:
  - Ilmenite processing: FeTiO3 + 2H2SO4 → FeSO4 + TiOSO4 + 2H2O
  - Selenium deposition: Na2SeO3 + H2SO4 → Se + Na2O + H2SO4 (recycled)
  - Acid leaching of minerals
  - Battery electrolyte (lead-acid batteries)
Stoichiometry:
  - Oxidation: 2SO2 (128g) + O2 (32g) → 2SO3 (160g)
  - Absorption: SO3 (80g) + H2O (18g) → H2SO4 (98g)
  - Overall: SO2 (64g) + 0.5 O2 (16g) + H2O (18g) → H2SO4 (98g)
Mass fractions: 153% H2SO4 from SO2 input
Equilibrium considerations:
  - Forward reaction favored at low temperature (exothermic)
  - But low temperature = slow kinetics
  - Compromise: 450°C with V2O5 catalyst
  - Multiple catalyst beds with interstage cooling for high conversion
Advantages: Highly exothermic (energy-positive process)
High conversion efficiency (>98%)
Acid not consumed in many applications (recycled)
Well-established industrial process
Disadvantages: Requires V2O5 catalyst (rare on Moon)
Highly corrosive product
SO2 from sulfur combustion or troilite (limited)
Lunar context: Sulfur/sulfuric acid scarce but essential
Used in selenium extraction (photosensitive material)
Ilmenite alternative processing route
Acid recycled in most processes (not consumed)
V2O5 catalyst import may be necessary
Sulfur source: Troilite from meteorites/regolith
Sustainable only if acid recycled, sulfur conserved

Steam reforming of methane to produce synthesis gas (syngas: CO + H2).
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Reaction: CH4 + H2O → CO + 3H2 (endothermic)
Temperature: 850°C

Purpose: First step in silicone plastic synthesis chain
Generate syngas for methanol production
Chemical feedstock for various syntheses
Process details:
  1. Methane (from lunar volatiles or Sabatier process)
  2. Superheated steam (H2O vapor)
  3. React over Ni catalyst at 850°C and 4 MPa
  4. CO and H2 produced (syngas)
  5. Separate syngas from unreacted steam
Products:
  - CO (carbon monoxide): Methanol synthesis, Fischer-Tropsch, Mond process
  - H2 (hydrogen): Reducing agent, fuel, chemical feedstock

High temperature and pressure requirements

  - Fischer-Tropsch: Syngas → hydrocarbons
  - Hydrogen production: Shift reaction CO + H2O → CO2 + H2
  - Chemical feedstock: Ammonia, methanol, aldehydes

raw.notes:
Basic thermionic converter for direct heat-to-electricity conversion.
Source: ellery-et-al-2022-metalysis-fray-farthing-chen-process, Power-on-the-Moon-using-ISRU.txt
Purpose: Convert waste heat from ISRU processes directly to electrical power
Efficiency: 15-20% typical (Russian nuclear reactors achieved 20%)
Temperature: 1500-2000°C cathode, 500-800°C anode
Simpler than PETE, suitable for waste heat recovery
Process details:
  1. High-temperature heat source (nuclear reactor, concentrated solar, or waste heat)
  2. Heat cathode to 1500-2000°C (thermionic emission temperature)
  3. Hot cathode emits electrons (thermionic emission)
  4. Richardson-Dushman equation: J = A·T² exp(-φ/kT)
     - J = current density (A/cm²)
     - A = Richardson constant (120 A/cm²/K² for free electrons)
     - T = absolute temperature (K)
     - φ = work function (eV)
     - k = Boltzmann constant
  5. Electrons travel across vacuum gap (~10-50 μm) to cooler anode
  6. Anode collects electrons (maintained at 500-800°C)
  7. External circuit returns electrons to cathode (generates power)
  8. Waste heat removed from anode via cooling system
  9. Continuous operation as long as heat source available
Products:
  - Electrical power: ~20% of input thermal energy
  - Low-temperature waste heat: ~80% (can be used for secondary processes)
Cathode materials and work functions:
  - Tungsten (W): φ = 4.5 eV (bare), requires very high temperature
  - Tungsten + BaO coating: φ = 1.8-2.0 eV (lower temperature operation)
  - Tungsten + CaO coating: φ = 1.6-1.8 eV (better performance)
  - Molybdenum: φ = 4.2 eV (alternative to tungsten)
  - Cesiated surfaces (Cs vapor): φ = 1.4-1.6 eV (best performance)
Anode materials:
  - Molybdenum: Good thermal conductivity, moderate work function
  - Nickel: Lower cost, adequate performance
  - Niobium: High-temperature capability
  - Work function less critical (electron collector)
Cathode coating production (lunar):
  - BaO: From barium_oxide_extraction_v0 process
  - CaO: From calcium_oxide_extraction_v0 process
  - Apply via vacuum deposition or spraying
  - Activate by heating in vacuum (drives off contaminants)
Operating principles:
  - Hot cathode: Thermal energy excites electrons over work function barrier
  - Vacuum gap: Electrons travel ballistically (no gas scattering)
  - Cold anode: Collects electrons, maintains voltage
  - Temperature difference: Drives thermodynamic efficiency
Efficiency equation:
  - Carnot limit: η_Carnot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot
  - With T_hot = 1800K, T_cold = 700K: η_Carnot = 61%
  - Practical thermionic: η = 15-20% (losses from work function, space charge)
Space charge effect:
  - Electron cloud builds up in gap (negative charge)
  - Repels additional electrons from cathode
  - Limits current density
  - Solutions:
    a) Close spacing (10-50 μm): Reduces space charge
    b) Cesium vapor: Positive ions neutralize electrons
    c) Magnetic field: Focuses electron beam
Cesium vapor mode (advanced):
  - Add Cs vapor to gap at low pressure (~1 torr)
  - Cs ionizes: Cs → Cs⁺ + e⁻
  - Cs⁺ ions neutralize electron space charge
  - Cs adsorbs on surfaces: Lowers work function
  - Significantly improves performance (20-25% efficiency)
  - Challenge: Cs vapor pressure control, containment
Temperature optimization:
  - Higher T_cathode: More emission, but higher losses
  - Lower T_anode: Higher voltage, but heat removal harder
  - Optimal: T_cathode = 1500-1800°C, T_anode = 500-700°C
Vacuum requirements:
  - High vacuum (10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁸ torr) prevents electron scattering
  - Or Cs vapor mode (1 torr Cs, controlled atmosphere)
  - Lunar surface: Natural high vacuum (~10⁻¹⁴ torr)
  - Simplifies vacuum envelope design
Gap spacing:
  - Small gap (10 μm): Reduces space charge, higher current
  - Large gap (100+ μm): Easier to fabricate, lower current
  - Typical: 20-50 μm for good performance
  - Precision alignment critical (thermal expansion)
Heat source options (lunar):
  - Nuclear reactor: Continuous high-temperature heat (fission)
  - Concentrated solar: Daytime operation only (heliostats, lenses)
  - Waste heat from FFC Cambridge: 900-1100°C (boost to 1500°C)
  - Waste heat from smelting: High-temperature industrial processes
Advantages: Direct conversion (no moving parts, no wear)
  Long lifetime (solid-state, no mechanical degradation)
  Compact and lightweight
  Silent operation
  Can use waste heat from ISRU processes
  Proven technology (Russian nuclear reactors, 1960s-1980s)
Disadvantages: Lower efficiency than PETE (20% vs 40-50%)
  Requires very high temperatures (1500-2000°C)
  Work function limits voltage output (~1-2V typical)
  Space charge limits current (unless mitigated)
  Materials challenges (high-temperature operation)
Lunar context: Abundant heat sources (solar, nuclear, ISRU waste heat)
  Natural high vacuum (simplifies design)
  Tungsten from meteorites (cathode material)
  BaO, CaO available from mineral processing
  Ideal for coupling with thermal ISRU processes
Russian TOPAZ reactor (space nuclear power):
  - Thermionic converter coupled to nuclear reactor
  - 5-10 kWe output (electrical)
  - 20% efficiency achieved
  - Operated in space (Cosmos satellites, 1960s-1980s)
  - Demonstrated long-term reliability (years)
Applications:
  - Nuclear reactor power systems: Base load (continuous)
  - Solar thermal power: Daytime peak load
  - Waste heat recovery: FFC Cambridge, smelting, glass melting
  - Combined heat and power (CHP): Electricity + process heat
Voltage and current characteristics:
  - Voltage: 0.5-1.5V per diode (limited by work function difference)
  - Current: 5-50 A/cm² (depends on temperature, spacing)
  - Power density: 2-20 W/cm² typical
  - Stack multiple diodes in series for higher voltage
Modular design:
  - Series connection: Increases voltage (N diodes × 1V = NV)
  - Parallel connection: Increases current
  - Typical module: 20-50 diodes in series (20-50V output)
  - Scale to desired power by number of modules
Cooling system (anode):
  - Heat pipes: Efficient heat transport
  - Liquid cooling: Water or molten salt loop
  - Radiative cooling: Large radiator area (space applications)
  - Lunar: Radiative cooling effective (no atmosphere)
Thermal management:
  - Cathode insulation: Minimize heat loss (high-temp insulation)
  - Anode cooling: Maximize heat extraction (fins, radiators)
  - Thermal cycling: Design for daily/seasonal temperature swings
Material degradation mechanisms:
  - Cathode evaporation: W, Mo evaporate at high temperatures
  - Coating depletion: BaO, CaO sublimate over time
  - Interdiffusion: Materials mix at high temperatures
  - Mitigation: Excess coating thickness, periodic renewal
Lifetime:
  - Well-designed: 5-10 years continuous operation
  - With maintenance (coating renewal): 20+ years
  - Russian TOPAZ: Operated for years in space
Comparison to other power systems:
  - Photovoltaic: 15-20% efficiency, lower temperature, lighter
  - Thermoelectric: 5-10% efficiency, simpler, lower temperature
  - Thermionic: 15-20% efficiency, high temperature, moderate complexity
  - PETE: 40-50% efficiency, high temperature, complex (photonic + thermionic)
  - Stirling engine: 30-40% efficiency, moving parts, wear
Integration with ISRU:
  - FFC Cambridge: 900-1100°C waste heat → boost to 1500°C → thermionic
  - Glass melting: 1400-1600°C furnace → thermionic on furnace walls
  - Smelting: 1500-2000°C operations → direct thermionic conversion
  - Net: Electrical power + useful heat for processes
Energy cascade (example):
  1. Concentrated solar → 2000°C
  2. Thermionic converter: 2000°C → 800°C, generate 20% electricity
  3. Waste heat (800°C) → FFC Cambridge (900°C with heat pump)
  4. FFC waste heat (700°C) → secondary processes
  5. Overall system efficiency: >60% useful energy
Power output scaling (example):
  - 100 kW thermal input
  - 20% efficiency → 20 kW electrical output
  - 80 kW waste heat at 700°C (reusable)
  - For 1 MW electrical: 5 MW thermal input required
Lunar deployment scenarios:
  - Near-polar bases: Solar concentrators on "peaks of eternal light"
  - Equatorial bases: Nuclear reactors for continuous power
  - Industrial sites: Waste heat recovery from smelters, furnaces
Research and development needs:
  - Long-term coating stability (BaO, CaO degradation)
  - Precision gap spacing control (thermal expansion compensation)
  - Cesium-free space charge mitigation (avoid Cs handling)
  - Integration with lunar heat sources (solar, nuclear, ISRU)
Recommended timeline:
  - Phase 1 (years 0-10): Use photovoltaics and batteries
  - Phase 2 (years 10-20): Deploy nuclear + thermionic for base load
  - Phase 3 (years 20-30): Integrate thermionic with ISRU waste heat
  - Phase 4 (years 30+): Transition to PETE for higher efficiency

raw.notes:
THERMIONIC SOLAR POWER GENERATION

Converts concentrated solar thermal energy (1600-2700°C) directly into electrical power
via thermionic emission in vacuum tube converters.

OPERATING PRINCIPLE:
- Concentrated sunlight heats tungsten cathode to emission temperature (~2000°C)
- Cathode coated with CaO to reduce work function and enable lower operating temperature
- Thermal energy causes thermionic emission - electrons "boil off" cathode surface
- Electrons flow across vacuum gap to nickel anode, generating DC electrical current
- No intermediate conversion steps (solar → thermal → electric directly)

CONVERSION EFFICIENCY:
- Primitive/v0 systems: ~10% solar-to-electric
- Optimized systems (v1/v2): 15-20%
- Theoretical maximum: 30%
- Waste heat: 70-90% must be rejected via radiators

ADVANTAGES OVER PHOTOVOLTAICS:
- 100% manufacturable from lunar materials (anorthite + NiFe meteorites)
- Higher efficiency than lunar PV (1-5% without dopants)
- Proven technology (used in space nuclear reactors: 5-20% efficiency)
- Dual-use concentrators (power + foundry operations)
- Same vacuum tube technology as computing/communications

MATERIALS (all lunar-sourced):
- Cathode: Tungsten with CaO coating (from anorthite)
- Anode: Nickel (from NiFe meteorites)
- Envelope: Fused silica glass (from anorthite)
- Concentrator: Cast glass Fresnel lenses or polished Ni mirrors

ENERGY FLOW:
Solar Irradiance → Concentrated Thermal (1600-2700°C) → Thermionic Emission
→ Electrical Power (10-30%) + Waste Heat (70-90%)

See design/solar_thermionics_report.md for complete technical specifications,
chemical processing equations, and references to source papers.

raw.notes:
Extraction of tungsten microparticles from NiFe meteorite material via density separation.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt, Lunar-Demandite.txt
Process: Grinding + hydrocyclone/centrifugal separation by density
Tungsten density: 19.3 g/cm³ (vs Fe: 7.87, Ni: 8.91 g/cm³)
Concentration: 0.1-5 μg/g (0.01-0.5 ppm) in NiFe meteorites
Purpose: Extract critical tungsten for tool steel and thermionic cathodes
Process details:
  1. NiFe meteorite residue (after Mond process for Ni/Fe extraction)
  2. Grind to fine powder in ball mill (<100 μm particles)
  3. Create water slurry with ground material
  4. Hydrocyclone separation:
     - Wet feed enters cyclone tangentially
     - Centrifugal forces push heavy particles (W) to walls
     - Heavy concentrate exits at bottom (underflow)
     - Light gangue exits at top (overflow)
  5. Multiple passes for concentration
  6. Dry tungsten concentrate
  7. Further purification if needed
Products:
  - Tungsten concentrate: W microparticles
  - Fe-Ni tailings: Iron-nickel residue (can be reprocessed)
  - Process water: Recycled
Density separation principles:
  - Stokes law: Settling velocity ∝ (ρparticle - ρfluid) × d²
  - Heavy tungsten particles settle faster
  - Centrifugal force enhances separation
  - Hydrocyclone provides compact, continuous operation
Tungsten in meteorites:
  - Present as micro-inclusions in NiFe metal
  - Concentration: 0.1-5 μg/g (extremely low)
  - Mass separation: 1 tonne meteorite → 0.1-5g tungsten
  - Challenging but critical extraction
Tungsten applications (critical):
  - Tool steel (Fe-W alloy): Cutting tools, drill bits, wear resistance
  - Thermionic cathodes: Vacuum tube electron emitters (heating elements)
  - High-temperature applications: Melting point 3422°C
  - Electrical contacts: High conductivity, durability
Stoichiometry: 1000 kg NiFe residue → ~0.5-5 kg W concentrate (0.05-0.5%)
Concentration factor: 100-1000× in concentrate vs feed
Alternative processing:
  - Magnetic separation (W non-magnetic, separate from Fe/Ni)
  - Flotation (surface chemistry differences)
  - Acid leaching (dissolve Fe/Ni, W remains)
Advantages: Uses density difference (19.3 vs 8 g/cm³)
  Simple mechanical separation
  No chemical reagents (water recycled)
  Works in lunar gravity (1/6 Earth, but still functional)
Disadvantages: Very low concentration (ppm level)
  Large mass throughput for small W output
  Multiple passes needed
  Requires fine grinding (energy intensive)
Lunar context: Tungsten absolutely critical but extremely scarce
  No tungsten minerals on Moon
  Meteorite impacts only source
  Magnetic anomalies indicate impact sites (NiFe meteorites)
  Must process large quantities for small yields
  Essential for tool steel and vacuum tube technology
Post-processing: Tungsten carbide formation (W + C → WC)
  - Used in cutting tools, abrasives
  - Harder than steel, very durable

raw.notes:
Water electrolysis for producing hydrogen and oxygen gases.
Source: All ISRU papers (fundamental process)
Reaction: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
Voltage: 1.23V minimum (thermodynamic), 1.8-2.4V typical (with overpotential)
Current density: 0.5-2 A/cm² typical
Purpose: Split water into constituent gases for propellant, life support, and chemical feedstock
Process details:
  1. Pure water (or dilute electrolyte solution)
  2. DC electrical current through electrolyzer cell
  3. Cathode reaction: 4H2O + 4e⁻ → 2H2 + 4OH⁻
  4. Anode reaction: 4OH⁻ → O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻
  5. Net: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
  6. H2 collected at cathode, O2 at anode
  7. Gas separation and drying
Products:
  - Hydrogen gas (H2): 11.1% by mass (stoichiometric)
  - Oxygen gas (O2): 88.9% by mass (stoichiometric)
Stoichiometry: 2H2O (36g) → 2H2 (4g) + O2 (32g)
Mass yields: 11.1% H2, 88.9% O2
Volume ratio: 2:1 (H2:O2) at STP
Electrolyte types:
  - Alkaline (KOH solution): Most common, mature technology
  - PEM (Proton Exchange Membrane): High purity, compact
  - Solid oxide (SOEC): High temperature, higher efficiency
Alkaline electrolysis (most common):
  - Electrolyte: 25-30% KOH solution
  - Temperature: 60-80°C
  - Pressure: 1-30 bar
  - Efficiency: 60-70% (LHV basis)
PEM electrolysis:
  - Membrane: Nafion or similar polymer
  - Temperature: 50-80°C
  - Pressure: Up to 200 bar (high-pressure H2)
  - Purity: 99.999% H2 (no KOH carryover)
  - Efficiency: 65-75%
Solid oxide electrolysis (SOEC):
  - Temperature: 700-900°C
  - Uses waste heat from other processes
  - Efficiency: 85-90% (thermoneutral operation)
  - Less mature technology
Energy requirements:
  - Theoretical minimum: 39.4 kWh/kg H2 (HHV basis)
  - Practical: 50-60 kWh/kg H2 (alkaline)
  - Per kg water: 4-5 kWh (typical)
Applications:
  - Propellant: H2-O2 rocket fuel (high Isp ~450s)
  - Life support: O2 for breathing
  - Chemical feedstock: H2 for reduction reactions
  - Energy storage: H2 fuel cells for power generation
  - Sabatier/Bosch: H2 for CO2 reduction
Lunar context: Critical process for ISRU
  - Water from polar ice or regolith volatiles
  - O2 for life support and oxidizer
  - H2 for propellant and chemical processing
  - Enables many downstream processes
Advantages: Simple, well-established technology
  High-purity products (especially PEM)
  Scalable from small to large scale
  No chemical reagents consumed
Disadvantages: Energy intensive
  Requires electrical power (solar/nuclear)
  Alkaline systems require KOH (Earth import initially)
  PEM membranes may be difficult to manufacture in-situ
Lunar implementation considerations:
  - PEM preferred for high purity and compactness
  - Alkaline viable with KOH import or in-situ synthesis
  - SOEC attractive if waste heat available (FFC, smelting)
  - High-pressure operation reduces storage volume
Gas purity and separation:
  - Membrane separators for final cleanup
  - H2 purity: 99.9-99.999% depending on electrolyzer type
  - O2 purity: 99.2-99.9%
  - Trace water removal via desiccant or PSA
Hydrogen storage:
  - Compressed gas: 200-700 bar tanks
  - Cryogenic liquid: 20K (-253°C)
  - Metal hydrides: Mg, LaNi5 (reversible storage)
Oxygen storage:
  - Compressed gas: 150-200 bar typical
  - Cryogenic liquid: 90K (-183°C)
  - Higher density as liquid (for propellant)
Safety considerations:
  - H2-O2 mixture explosive (4-75% H2 in O2)
  - Must prevent gas mixing
  - Catalytic recombiners for trace H2 removal from O2
  - Proper venting in case of overpressure
Efficiency improvements:
  - Advanced catalysts: IrO2 (anode), Pt (cathode) for PEM
  - Thinner membranes: Reduce resistance
  - Higher temperature: Improves kinetics (SOEC)
  - Pressurized operation: Direct high-pressure H2
Integration opportunities:
  - Coupled with FFC Cambridge: O2 from both processes
  - Sabatier loop: Recycle H2 from water product
  - Fuel cells: Reverse process for power generation
  - Ilmenite reduction: H2 feedstock for reduction

raw.notes:
Zone refining for achieving extreme purity levels in silicon for semiconductors.
Source: Sustainable-ISRU-on-the-Moon.txt
Process: Thermal zone melting with impurity segregation
Temperature: ~1600°C (local melting zone)
Purpose: Achieve 9-11 nines purity (99.9999999-99.999999999% pure)
Essential for semiconductor manufacturing
Process details:
  1. Silicon ingot from Siemens process (polycrystalline)
  2. Mount in horizontal apparatus
  3. RF induction coil creates narrow molten zone (~1 cm wide)
  4. Slowly translate molten zone along ingot (mm/hr)
  5. Impurities preferentially stay in liquid phase
  6. Solid crystallizes behind zone with lower impurity
  7. Multiple passes (10-50) progressively concentrate impurities
  8. Cut off impure ends, recycle to earlier processing
Physical principle: Distribution coefficient k = Csolid/Cliquid
  - For most impurities in Si: k < 1 (reject into liquid)
  - Examples: B (k=0.8), P (k=0.35), Al (k=0.002)
  - Impurities swept to end of ingot
Products:
  - Ultra-pure silicon: Center section of ingot
  - Impure ends: Recycled to Siemens process (modeled as silicon_purified)
Purity levels achievable:
  - Starting: 99.9999% (6 nines, from Siemens)
  - After 10 passes: 99.9999999% (9 nines)
  - After 30-50 passes: 99.999999999% (11 nines)
Critical impurities removed:
  - Boron (p-type dopant): Must control to <0.1 ppb
  - Phosphorus (n-type dopant): Must control to <0.1 ppb
  - Transition metals (Fe, Cu, Ni): Recombination centers
  - Carbon: Forms SiC defects
Advantages: Achieves extreme purity levels
  No chemical reagents required
  Physics-based separation (thermodynamic)
  Scalable to large ingots
Disadvantages: Very slow process (days per ingot)
  Energy intensive (maintain molten zone)
  Requires multiple passes for highest purity
  ~2% material loss to impure ends per pass
Lunar context: Essential for electronics manufacturing
  Semiconductor devices require 9+ nines purity
  Photovoltaics can use lower purity (6-7 nines)
  Zone refining is final purification step
Alternative: Czochralski pulling also achieves high purity
  But zone refining can reach even higher levels
Process variations:
  - Vertical zone refining (better for vacuum)
  - Horizontal (shown here, easier mechanically)
  - Float-zone (contactless, highest purity)
Yield: 98% ultra-pure silicon per pass
  Impure ends (2%) recycled to Siemens or earlier
Temperature control critical:
  - Too hot: Excessive evaporation, Si loss
  - Too cold: Zone freezes, process stops
  - Must maintain 1600°C ± 10°C in zone
Atmosphere: Inert (Ar) or vacuum
  Prevents oxidation and contamination
Post-processing: Czochralski growth into single crystal
  Or direct use as polycrystalline for some applications

raw.notes:
Manufactures electric parallel gripper from lunar materials + imported motor.

Design: 2-finger parallel jaw, 120mm stroke, 200N gripping force.
Aluminum body, steel ball screw, imported stepper motor and bearings.

Process:
1. Cast aluminum gripper body housing
2. CNC machine precision features:
   - Parallel finger slides with linear bearings
   - Ball screw mounting and nut
   - Motor mounting flange
3. Fabricate ball screw from lunar steel (10mm dia, 5mm pitch)
4. Assemble components:
   - Install 4 linear bearings for finger slides
   - Mount ball screw and nut
   - Attach NEMA 23 stepper motor (imported)
   - Install interchangeable jaw inserts
5. Test stroke, gripping force, repeatability

Inputs:
- 4.5 kg aluminum (4 kg final + scrap)
- 0.5 kg steel for ball screw
- 1× stepper motor (NEMA 23, imported - requires magnets)
- 4× linear bearings (imported in Phase 1)
- Fasteners for assembly

Lunar manufacturability: Body and ball screw from lunar materials.
Motor and precision bearings imported (require NdFeB magnets and precision balls).

Phase 2: Manufacture bearings from lunar materials with precision grinding.

Design reference: docs/labor_bot_design_memo.md section 3.6.1.

Requires extreme precision - way straightness and flatness within ±0.005-0.01 mm over full length, parallelism between ways within ±0.01 mm. Critical component determining lathe accuracy. Casting must be stress-relieved for dimensional stability. Final precision achieved by hand scraping ways - traditional machine tool building technique. Most time-consuming and skill-intensive component of lathe construction. Accuracy of this component determines turning precision of entire lathe.

raw.notes:
Import recipe for nitrile rubber (NBR).

Nitrile rubber production requires:
1. Butadiene monomer (from petroleum cracking)
2. Acrylonitrile monomer (from propylene/ammonia)
3. Emulsion polymerization reactors
4. Coagulation and drying equipment

Challenges for lunar production:
- No petroleum sources on Moon (hydrocarbons must be synthesized)
- Complex petrochemical processing chain
- Energy-intensive synthesis

Alternatives for local production:
- Silicone rubber (from lunar silicon + methane)
- Fluoroelastomers (if fluorine available)
- EPDM from synthesized ethylene/propylene

Marked as import for bootstrap phase. Consider silicone rubber as locally-manufacturable alternative.
